0.1.title: What an embedded system is, and the anatomy of your ESP32-S3
0.1.status: draft: firmware not yet built in CI
0.1.body:
## Why this matters

Every later lesson assumes you can get code onto a board and read what it says back. The boot log you will read today is the same log you will read when a product resets in the field at 3 a.m.; engineers who can read it find faults in minutes.

## Prerequisites, hardware, time

- One ESP32-S3 N16R8 board and a USB data cable (many cables are charge-only)
- A computer with about 5 GB free
- 60 to 90 minutes, most of it the toolchain download

No wiring. No other parts.

## Build it first

Work through this list; your ticks are saved.

- [ ] Install one toolchain. ESP-IDF directly: `eim install -i v6.1`. Or PlatformIO: install the VS Code extension; it fetches its own ESP-IDF on the first build
- [ ] Open a terminal in `firmware/phase0/0.1-hello` (for ESP-IDF, one with its environment active)
- [ ] Plug the board in through the port marked UART or COM, if it has two
- [ ] Build, flash and open the monitor. ESP-IDF: `idf.py set-target esp32s3`, then `idf.py flash monitor`. PlatformIO: `pio run -e esp32s3 -t upload -t monitor`
- [ ] Find the three lines printed by your own code in the output
- [ ] Leave the monitor: `Ctrl+]` under ESP-IDF, `Ctrl+C` under PlatformIO

Every later lesson says “build and flash” and means either of these. The [toolchain cheatsheet](#sheets-toolchains) lists each command side by side.

The whole program:

```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <inttypes.h>
#include "sdkconfig.h"
#include "freertos/FreeRTOS.h"
#include "freertos/task.h"
#include "esp_chip_info.h"
#include "esp_system.h"

void app_main(void)
{
    esp_chip_info_t chip;
    esp_chip_info(&chip);

    printf("Hello from %s: %d core(s), silicon revision v%d.%d\n",
           CONFIG_IDF_TARGET, chip.cores, chip.revision / 100, chip.revision % 100);
    printf("Free heap: %" PRIu32 " bytes\n", esp_get_free_heap_size());

    for (int tick = 0; ; tick++) {
        printf("tick %d\n", tick);
        vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(1000));
    }
}
```

After roughly forty lines of boot log, your own output appears. The revision and heap numbers vary by board:

```expected
Hello from esp32s3: 2 core(s), silicon revision v<major>.<minor>
Free heap: <a few hundred thousand> bytes
tick 0
tick 1
tick 2
```

If nothing appears, see “Common mistakes” at the end before changing any code.

## How it works

**Four kinds of chip.** The words are used loosely in job postings; this is what they mean.

| | What it is | Memory | Runs | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MCU, microcontroller | CPU, RAM, flash and peripherals in one package | Kilobytes to a few megabytes | Bare metal or an RTOS | STM32F4, ATmega328 |
| MPU, microprocessor | A CPU that needs external RAM and storage | Hundreds of megabytes and up | Linux or another full OS | The chip in a Raspberry Pi |
| SoC, system on chip | A CPU plus radios or other large subsystems on one die | Either scale | Depends on the chip | ESP32-S3 (MCU-class), Jetson’s Orin (MPU-class) |
| FPGA | Logic you configure into a circuit, not a program you run | Not applicable | Your own digital design | Lattice iCE40 |

Your ESP32-S3 is an MCU-class SoC: a microcontroller with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth LE radios built in.

**What is inside your board.** “N16R8” is the module’s memory option: 16 MB of flash for code and files, 8 MB of PSRAM as extra, slower RAM. The chip itself has two Xtensa LX7 cores at up to 240 MHz and 512 KB of fast internal RAM. Confirm these in the ESP32-S3 Series Datasheet, section “Features”; reading that page is part of lesson 0.6.

Select any block to see what it is for and where the course returns to it.

::widget chip

**What the boot log is telling you.** Three programs run in sequence, and each prints its own section:

1. **ROM bootloader.** Code fixed in the chip at the factory. It prints why the chip reset and which boot mode the strapping pins selected, then loads the next stage from flash.
2. **Second-stage bootloader.** Built from ESP-IDF source along with your app. It prints its version, the flash settings and the partition table, then picks an application and loads its segments.
3. **Your application.** ESP-IDF start-up code initialises the heap, the clocks and FreeRTOS, starts a task called `main`, and that task calls your `app_main()`. Look for a line from `main_task` just before your “Hello”.

Step through the same sequence here, then find each stage in your own log.

::widget boot

So `app_main` is not where execution starts. It is a function called by a FreeRTOS task that the framework created for you, which is why `vTaskDelay` works inside it.

## Go deeper

Scroll back through the log and answer these from what is printed; write the answers in your notebook.

- [ ] What reset reason does the ROM report after you press the board’s reset button? After you unplug and replug it?
- [ ] How many partitions are listed, and at what offset does the application start?
- [ ] How large is the application image? Run `idf.py size` and find the same number.
- [ ] Comment out the `vTaskDelay` line, rebuild and flash. What changes after a few seconds, and what does the new message name?

That last experiment is your first watchdog reset. A task that never yields starves the idle task, and the task watchdog reports it. Lesson 2.10 covers watchdogs properly.

## When to use it, when not to

| You need | Reach for | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A sensor node on a battery, wireless, under a few dollars | An MCU-class SoC such as the ESP32-S3 | Microamp sleep currents, instant start, deterministic timing |
| A camera pipeline at 30 frames per second with a large neural network | An MPU-class system such as a Jetson | Gigabytes of RAM, a GPU, Linux drivers |
| Sub-microsecond parallel signal processing | An FPGA | Hardware parallelism, no instruction-by-instruction execution |
| A user interface with a browser and a filesystem full of apps | An MPU running Linux | The software ecosystem |

The boundary you will explore in Phase 9: an ESP32-S3 can run a person detector in tens of milliseconds, but not a large vision model.

## Break it

Do each of these on purpose and record the exact message you get. These three faults account for most “my board is dead” posts.

- [ ] Build for the wrong chip: `idf.py set-target esp32`, build, and try to flash the S3. Read what the flasher reports, then set the target back.
- [ ] Open a second serial monitor while the first is running, then try to flash.
- [ ] Use a charge-only USB cable, if you own one, and note what your computer does and does not show.

## Check yourself

The Phase 0 quiz includes questions on this lesson. Before taking it, answer aloud:

1. Which of the three boot stages can you change, and which can you not?
2. Why does a line from `main_task` appear before your own output?
3. What does “N16R8” tell you, and which part of it is flash?

## Stretch goals

- Print the reset reason from your own code with `esp_reset_reason()` and trigger three different ones.
- Change the tick period to 100 ms and estimate, from the timestamps in the monitor, how accurate it is.

## Reading

- *Making Embedded Systems*, 2nd edition, chapter 1
- ESP-IDF Programming Guide for v6.1: “Get Started” and “Application Startup Flow”
- ESP32-S3 Series Datasheet: the first two pages

## Common mistakes and interview angles

- **Nothing happens when flashing.** The cable is charge-only, or the board is on its native-USB port and your system needs a driver or a different port. Try the other USB connector if the board has two.
- **The port is busy.** Another program, usually a second monitor, holds the serial port.
- **Garbage characters in the monitor.** The monitor’s baud rate does not match the console’s. `idf.py monitor` reads the right value from the project; a separate terminal program does not.
- **Interview angle.** “Walk me through what happens between power-on and `main()`” is a standard opener. A good answer names the ROM, the bootloader, start-up code that sets up memory and clocks, and then the application, and says which of those you have changed in practice.

0.10.body:
## Why this matters

“It works, but it feels slow”, “it drops a sample every few seconds” and “it hangs when the sensor is unplugged” are timing-design faults, not coding faults. This lesson gives you the vocabulary to design them out.

## Prerequisites, hardware, time

Lesson 0.9 and its firmware. 45 minutes.

## Build it first

Open the jitter lab again, choose vTaskDelay, and sweep the requested period from 1 ms to 50 ms. Watch the mean error.

::widget jitter

- [ ] At which requested periods is vTaskDelay exact? What do they have in common?
- [ ] What happens below 10 ms, and why does nothing warn you?
- [ ] On the board: in `0.9-wait` mode 1 (busy loop), raise the wait to 2 seconds and watch the log. Something complains. Write down what it names

## How it works

**Latency and throughput.** Latency is how long one thing takes from cause to effect. Throughput is how many things get done per second. They pull against each other: batching ten samples before processing raises throughput and makes the first sample wait. A control loop cares about latency; a data logger cares about throughput. Decide which you are building.

**Blocking and busy-waiting.** A busy-wait keeps the CPU spinning until time passes. Nothing else at the same or lower priority can run, the idle task cannot run, and the watchdog you just triggered is the system telling you so. A blocking delay hands the CPU back to the scheduler until the time is up. On a battery the difference is also power: the idle task is what lets the chip sleep.

**The tick.** The scheduler measures time in ticks, 10 ms each by default in ESP-IDF. `vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(25))` waits 2 ticks, not 25 ms, and `pdMS_TO_TICKS(5)` is zero. For anything finer than a tick you need a hardware timer.

**Two kinds of clock.** *Monotonic* time counts up from boot and never jumps: use it for intervals, timeouts and scheduling. *Wall-clock* time is the date and time of day; it is set from outside, by a network or a user, and can jump forwards or backwards when corrected. Measuring an interval with wall-clock time is a bug that appears on the day the clock is adjusted.

**Timeouts.** Any wait for something outside your control (a sensor, a network, a human) must have a limit and a plan for when the limit passes. A loop that waits for a pin to go high is a hang waiting for a loose wire.

```c
int64_t start = esp_timer_get_time();            /* microseconds since boot, monotonic */
while (gpio_get_level(ECHO_GPIO) == 0) {
    if (esp_timer_get_time() - start > 30000) {  /* 30 ms: no echo is coming */
        return ESP_ERR_TIMEOUT;
    }
}
```

**Under the hood.** `esp_timer_get_time()` reads the 64-bit SYSTIMER counter and divides by 16; `vTaskDelay` parks the task on the delayed list; `esp_rom_delay_us` spins in ROM. Lesson 0.14 follows each of them to the hardware, and the [under-the-hood cheatsheet](#sheets-under-the-hood) keeps the rows.

## Go deeper

- [ ] The HC-SR04 holds ECHO high for at most a few tens of milliseconds. Use the echo lab to choose a timeout for a 4 m range, with margin.
- [ ] A task must run every 10 ms and its work takes 3 ms. If it ends with `vTaskDelay` of one tick, what is its real period? Lesson 4.2 introduces the call that fixes this.
- [ ] List every place in your lesson 0.7 and 0.8 firmware that would hang if a wire came loose.

## When to use it, when not to

| Waiting for | Use | Never |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A fixed, long interval | `vTaskDelay` | A busy loop |
| An event from an interrupt | Block on a queue or notification with a timeout (Phase 4) | Polling a flag in a tight loop |
| A pin, inside a protocol, for microseconds | A bounded busy-wait | An unbounded one |
| A date and time | Wall-clock time | Wall-clock time for measuring intervals |

## Break it

- [ ] Unplug the jumper from lesson 0.8’s firmware and add a loop that waits for the pin to go high. Watch it hang, then add the timeout.

## Check yourself

1. Give one product that needs low latency and one that needs high throughput.
2. Why is `pdMS_TO_TICKS(5)` dangerous at the default tick rate?
3. Your interval timer runs backwards once a year. What kind of clock did you use?

## Stretch goals

- Change the tick rate to 1000 Hz in menuconfig and repeat the vTaskDelay measurement. What did you gain and what does it cost?
- Write `wait_for_level(pin, level, timeout_us)` and reuse it in every later lesson.

## Reading

- ESP-IDF Programming Guide: “ESP Timer (High Resolution Timer)” and the FreeRTOS overview
- *Making Embedded Systems*, “Managing the Flow of Activity”

## Common mistakes and interview angles

- **A wait with no timeout.** The most common cause of a device that “freezes sometimes”.
- **Treating the tick as a millisecond.** It is whatever the configuration says.
- **Interview angle.** “Why is `delay()` considered bad practice?” Separate the two cases: a busy-wait is harmful; a blocking delay is fine but coarse and must never be how you measure time.

0.11.body:
## Why this matters

Registers are bits. Protocol frames are bits. Half of all firmware bugs are a wrong mask, a wrong shift or a byte order mismatch, and almost every embedded interview opens with one of these on a whiteboard.

## Prerequisites, hardware, time

A C compiler on your computer (gcc or clang). No board. 60 minutes.

## Build it first

Use the playground until each of these takes you under ten seconds. Predict first, then click.

::widget bits

- [ ] Start from 0. Set bits 0, 3 and 7. What is the value in hex?
- [ ] Clear bit 3 without touching the others. Which operation and mask did it use?
- [ ] Enter `0xFF`. What is the low byte as a signed 8-bit number?
- [ ] Enter `0x12345678`. In what order do the bytes sit in memory on your ESP32?
- [ ] Shift `0x80000000` left by one. Where did the bit go?

Then the same in C, on your computer:

```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdint.h>

int main(void)
{
    uint32_t reg = 0;
    reg |=  (1u << 3);                 /* set bit 3            */
    reg |=  (1u << 7) | (1u << 0);     /* set bits 7 and 0     */
    reg &= ~(1u << 3);                 /* clear bit 3          */
    reg ^=  (1u << 0);                 /* toggle bit 0         */
    printf("0x%02X  bit7=%u\n", (unsigned)reg, (unsigned)((reg >> 7) & 1u));
    return 0;
}
```

```expected
0x80  bit7=1
```

## How it works

**Hexadecimal** is shorthand for binary: one hex digit is exactly four bits. `0xA5` is `1010 0101`. Registers are written in hex because you can see the bits through it.

**The four operations.** OR with a mask sets bits. AND with the inverted mask clears them. XOR toggles. Shift-and-AND reads one out. Everything else is a combination.

**Fields.** Registers often pack several small numbers into one word. To write a 3-bit field at bits 6 to 4:

```c
#define MODE_SHIFT  4
#define MODE_MASK   (0x7u << MODE_SHIFT)
reg = (reg & ~MODE_MASK) | ((value << MODE_SHIFT) & MODE_MASK);
```

Clear the field, then OR in the new value. Forgetting the clear is the classic bug: it works until the new value has a 0 where the old one had a 1.

**Two’s complement.** Signed integers store negative numbers so that ordinary addition works: invert the bits and add one. In eight bits, −1 is `0xFF` and −128 is `0x80`. The top bit tells you the sign, which is why reading a sensor’s signed 16-bit register into an unsigned variable gives 65,000 instead of −500.

**Endianness.** A 32-bit value occupies four bytes; which comes first is a convention. Your ESP32, and nearly every modern microcontroller, is little-endian: least significant byte at the lowest address. Many sensors and all network protocols send the most significant byte first. Joining two bytes from a sensor is therefore always explicit:

```c
int16_t accel_x = (int16_t)((uint16_t)buf[0] << 8 | buf[1]);   /* big-endian on the wire */
```

## Go deeper

- [ ] Why `1u << 3` and not `1 << 3`? Try `1 << 31` with warnings enabled (`-Wall -Wextra`) and read the result.
- [ ] Write `set_field(reg, shift, width, value)` and test it against five cases you worked by hand.
- [ ] A status register reads `0x5A`. Bits 7 to 5 are an error code, bit 4 is “busy”, bits 3 to 0 are a count. Extract all three.

## When to use it, when not to

| Task | Idiom |
| --- | --- |
| One flag | `reg |= BIT`, `reg &= ~BIT`, `if (reg & BIT)` |
| A multi-bit field | Mask and shift, as above |
| Bytes from a wire into a number | Explicit shifts, never a pointer cast |
| Describing a register layout | Masks and shifts, not C bitfields: their layout is up to the compiler (lesson 1.4) |

## Break it

Each of these compiles. Find what is wrong before running it.

```c
uint8_t status = 0x90;
if (status & 0x80 == 0x80) { /* ... */ }      /* 1 */
uint32_t mask = 1 << 31;                      /* 2 */
int8_t t = buf[0] << 8 | buf[1];              /* 3 */
```

- [ ] One is an operator-precedence trap, one is undefined behaviour, one throws away half the data. Which is which?

## Check yourself

The Phase 0 quiz covers masks, two’s complement, wrap-around and byte order. Before it:

1. What mask clears bits 4 and 5 and leaves the rest?
2. What is `0xFE` as a signed 8-bit number?
3. A sensor sends `0x12` then `0x34` for a 16-bit value. What is it?

## Stretch goals

- Write `popcount`, `reverse_bits` and `is_power_of_two` three ways each. These are interview favourites.
- Read a 12-bit value that straddles two bytes: the top eight bits in one, the low four in the high nibble of the next.

## Reading

- *Effective C*, the chapters on integer types and on expressions and operators
- *The C Programming Language*, section 2.9 on bitwise operators

## Common mistakes and interview angles

- **`==` binds tighter than `&`.** Always parenthesise the mask test.
- **Shifting into or past the sign bit of a signed type.** Use unsigned constants.
- **Assuming byte order.** State it in a comment next to every multi-byte read.
- **Interview angle.** “Set bit 5, clear bit 3, toggle bit 0 of this register without disturbing the rest.” Say the idiom aloud as you write it.

## Why this matters

Sensors hand you integers that mean fractions. Small processors do float arithmetic slowly or not at all, and a quantized neural network is fixed-point arithmetic in a long coat. And every byte you send over a wire can arrive wrong, so every real protocol carries a check.

## Prerequisites, hardware, time

Lesson 0.11. A C compiler on your computer. 75 minutes.

## Build it first

Type `0.1` into the lab and look at the error. Then try `16777217`.

::widget float

- [ ] What value does a float really store for 0.1? How large is the error?
- [ ] Why can a float not hold 16,777,217? What is the gap between neighbours there?
- [ ] Click the top exponent bit of 1.0. What happened to the value, and why by that much?
- [ ] Set the fixed-point format to Q8.8 and enter 3.3. What integer is stored, and what is the error?

Now protect some data. Enter a short message and watch the register change with each byte:

::widget crc

- [ ] Select CRC-8 and type `123456789`. The result should be the published check value, 0xF4
- [ ] Change one character. How much of the result changed?
- [ ] Switch to CRC-8/MAXIM, the one the DS18B20 uses in Phase 3. Same data, different answer: why?

## How it works

**Floating point** stores a sign, an exponent and 24 bits of precision. The precision is relative: about seven significant decimal digits wherever the value sits. That makes it convenient and gives it three traps. Most decimal fractions are not exact. Large values lose the ability to represent small steps. And comparing two floats for equality after arithmetic usually fails.

**On a microcontroller**, a `float` is cheap only if the chip has a floating-point unit. Your ESP32-S3 has a single-precision one; `double` is done in software and is much slower. Many smaller chips have neither.

**Fixed point** is an integer with an agreed scale. In Q8.8 the stored integer is the real value times 256. Addition is ordinary addition. Multiplication needs one shift afterwards:

```c
typedef int16_t q8_8_t;
#define Q(x)  ((q8_8_t)((x) * 256.0f + ((x) >= 0 ? 0.5f : -0.5f)))

static inline q8_8_t q_mul(q8_8_t a, q8_8_t b)
{
    return (q8_8_t)(((int32_t)a * b) >> 8);     /* widen first, then rescale */
}
```

The step is constant, the cost is integer arithmetic, and overflow is yours to prevent. Sensor datasheets speak fixed point constantly: “divide the raw value by 16384 to get g” is Q2.14.

**Checksums and CRCs.** A checksum adds the bytes up; it is cheap and misses reordered bytes and many double errors. A CRC treats the message as one long binary number and keeps the remainder of dividing it by a fixed polynomial. It catches every single-bit error, every burst shorter than its width, and almost everything else. Two ends must agree on five things, not one: the polynomial, the starting value, whether bytes are bit-reversed going in, whether the result is reversed, and a final XOR. That is why the same polynomial appears under several names.

## Go deeper

Write CRC-8 (polynomial 0x07, start 0) twice in C on your computer and check both against the lab.

- [ ] Bit by bit: for each byte, XOR it into the register, then eight times shift left and XOR with 0x07 whenever the bit shifted out was 1
- [ ] Table-driven: precompute the 256 results of doing that to every possible byte, then process one byte per lookup
- [ ] Time both on a megabyte of data. What did the table cost in memory?

## When to use it, when not to

| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Quick arithmetic on a chip with an FPU, modest precision | `float` |
| Money, counters, timestamps, anything compared for equality | Integers |
| DSP or ML on a chip without an FPU, or for speed and determinism | Fixed point |
| Detecting a corrupted frame | CRC; 8 bits for short frames, 16 or 32 for longer ones |
| Detecting deliberate tampering | Not a CRC: a cryptographic MAC (lesson 5.10) |

## Break it

```c
float total = 0.0f;
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) total += 0.1f;
if (total == 1.0f) puts("ten tenths make one");
```

- [ ] Predict whether it prints. Run it. Then fix the comparison properly.
- [ ] Multiply two Q8.8 values without widening to 32 bits first. Find inputs that give a wrong answer.

## Check yourself

1. How many significant decimal digits does a float hold?
2. What integer represents 1.5 in Q8.8?
3. Name two parameters of a CRC besides its polynomial.

## Stretch goals

- Convert a raw MPU6050 accelerometer reading to g in fixed point with no floats at all.
- Find the CRC used by Modbus RTU in the lab’s list and note how it differs from CCITT.

## Reading

- “What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic”, David Goldberg; read the first third
- *Making Embedded Systems*, the chapter on doing mathematics on small processors

## Common mistakes and interview angles

- **`==` on floats.** Compare against a tolerance, or use integers.
- **`double` by accident.** An unsuffixed constant such as `0.1` is a double in C; write `0.1f`.
- **CRC mismatch.** Almost always the reflect or initial-value setting, not the polynomial.
- **Interview angle.** “Implement a CRC” or “why not just use a checksum?” Know one concrete failure a checksum misses: two swapped bytes.

0.13.body:
## Why this matters

Every driver, on every chip, ends in a write to a memory address. `gpio_set_level()` is a convenience; underneath is one store instruction. Engineers who have done it by hand once can read any vendor’s code, debug with a register dump, and move to an STM32 without fear.

## Prerequisites, hardware, time

An LED and resistor on GPIO4 of an S3 board (or the ESP32-CAM, whose flash LED is on GPIO4: bright, do not look into it). Lessons 0.4 and 0.11. The ESP32-S3 Technical Reference Manual. 75 minutes.

## Build it first

Drive the LEDs in the model by writing registers. Try to light pins 0 and 2 without disturbing pin 1, three different ways.

::widget reg

- [ ] Write `0x05` to OUT. Then set pin 1 using OUT alone. What did you have to know first?
- [ ] Do the same with OUT_W1TS. What did you not have to know?
- [ ] Write `0x03` to ENABLE. Which LEDs went dark although their OUT bits are still 1?
- [ ] Run the interrupt race both ways and read the log

Now the real chip:

- [ ] Open the Technical Reference Manual, chapter “IO MUX and GPIO Matrix”, and find the register summary
- [ ] Write down the addresses of `GPIO_OUT_REG`, `GPIO_OUT_W1TS_REG`, `GPIO_OUT_W1TC_REG` and `GPIO_ENABLE_REG`
- [ ] Build and flash `firmware/phase0/0.13-registers`. The LED blinks with no driver call in the loop

```c
#include "soc/soc.h"        /* REG_WRITE, BIT */
#include "soc/gpio_reg.h"   /* GPIO_OUT_W1TS_REG and friends */

    for (;;) {
        REG_WRITE(GPIO_OUT_W1TS_REG, BIT(LED_GPIO));   /* one store: pin high */
        vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(250));
        REG_WRITE(GPIO_OUT_W1TC_REG, BIT(LED_GPIO));   /* one store: pin low  */
        vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(250));
    }
```

```expected
OUT register after set:   bit 4 = 1
OUT register after clear: bit 4 = 0
```

## How it works

**Memory-mapped I/O.** The CPU has one address space. Some addresses lead to RAM, some to flash, and some to peripheral registers: storage whose bits are wired to hardware. Writing a 1 to the right bit at the right address raises a pin’s voltage. Reading an address can return a pin’s level, a counter’s value or a received byte. To the CPU it is all loads and stores.

**What `REG_WRITE` is.** In essence, a macro that casts a number to a pointer and stores through it:

```c
#define REG_WRITE(addr, val)  (*(volatile uint32_t *)(addr) = (val))
```

`volatile` tells the compiler that this location can change by itself and that every access matters, so it must not optimise any away. Lesson 1.3 returns to it.

**Why set and clear registers exist.** `OUT |= mask` is read, modify, write. If an interrupt changes the register between your read and your write, its change is lost. `W1TS` and `W1TC` (“write one to set”, “write one to clear”) change only the bits you name in a single store, so nothing can come between.

**What the driver was doing for you.** `gpio_set_direction` sets the pin’s bit in the enable register. `gpio_reset_pin` also selects the GPIO function for that pin in the IO MUX, because a pin can belong to several peripherals. The lab keeps those two calls and replaces only the loop; the stretch goal replaces the direction too.

**The same idea on another chip.** The classic ESP32 has registers with the same names at different addresses. An STM32 calls them `ODR`, `BSRR` and `MODER`. The names change; the three ideas (output value, atomic set and clear, direction) do not.

## Go deeper

- [ ] Read `GPIO_OUT_REG` back with `REG_READ` after each write and print bit 4, as in the expected output.
- [ ] Pins 32 and above live in a second set of registers. Find their names in the reference manual. Which register and bit would you write for GPIO33?
- [ ] Find the same four registers for the classic ESP32 in its own reference manual. Record both addresses side by side.
- [ ] Toggle the pin in a tight loop with no delay and measure the frequency on the logic analyzer. Then do it with `gpio_set_level`. How much does the driver cost?

## When to use it, when not to

| Situation | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Application code | The driver. It is portable, checked and thread-safe |
| The tightest loop of a bit-banged protocol | Direct register writes, once measured to matter |
| Understanding or debugging a peripheral | Read the registers, in code or from the debugger |
| A peripheral the driver does not cover | Registers, wrapped in your own small HAL |

## Break it

- [ ] Remove the `gpio_set_direction` call and run it. The OUT bit toggles when you read it back, yet the LED stays dark. Explain, using the model’s ENABLE register.
- [ ] Replace `W1TS` with `REG_WRITE(GPIO_OUT_REG, BIT(LED_GPIO))`. It appears to work. What did you just do to every other pin?

## Check yourself

1. What does “memory-mapped” mean in one sentence?
2. Why is `REG |= mask` unsafe when interrupts use the same register?
3. A pin’s output bit is 1 but the pin measures 0 V. Name two registers to check.

## Stretch goals

- Replace `gpio_set_direction` with a write to `GPIO_ENABLE_W1TS_REG`.
- Make the project build for both chips, with the pin and any differing register chosen by `#if CONFIG_IDF_TARGET_ESP32S3`.
- Start your own header, `reg.h`, with `REG_SET_BITS`, `REG_CLR_BITS` and a field-write macro from lesson 0.11.

## Reading

- ESP32-S3 Technical Reference Manual: “IO MUX and GPIO Matrix”
- *Making Embedded Systems*, the chapter on inputs, outputs and registers

## Common mistakes and interview angles

- **Writing the whole register to change one pin.** It works on the bench with one LED and breaks the product.
- **Forgetting the direction or the function select.** The value is right and the pin does nothing.
- **Interview angle.** “What happens when you call `gpio_set_level`?” Walk down the layers: driver function, register macro, store to a memory-mapped address, a latch, an output transistor, the pin.

0.14.body:
## Why this matters

A driver call is a promise that something happens in silicon. Until you know what it is, you cannot predict what the call costs, whether it is safe in an interrupt, why a pin reads 0, or what breaks when two pieces of code share a pin. This lesson takes one small, real program, an ultrasonic ranger with an RGB LED, and follows every call in it down to the register it touches. From here on, every lesson ends its “How it works” with an **Under the hood** table for each new call, and the [under-the-hood cheatsheet](#sheets-under-the-hood) collects them.

## Prerequisites, hardware, time

- An HC-SR04 or HY-SRF05 with the 1 kΩ over 2 kΩ divider on ECHO (lesson 0.5), a common-anode RGB LED with three resistors, an S3 board
- Lesson 0.13 (registers), lesson 0.10 (timeouts)
- The ESP-IDF source on your disk. With PlatformIO it is in `~/.platformio/packages/framework-espidf/` (on Windows, `%USERPROFILE%\.platformio\packages\framework-espidf\`)
- 3 hours

## Build it first

Write the ranger yourself before looking at the reference: ping, time the echo, print the distance, light the LED red when something is nearer than 30 cm.

| S3 pin | Connects to | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GPIO18 | TRIG | 3.3 V is enough to trigger it |
| GPIO17 | ECHO, through the divider | Never 5 V straight into the pin. Not GPIO19 or 20: those are USB |
| GPIO4, 5, 21 | Red, green, blue cathodes, each through a resistor | Common anode to 3.3 V |
| 5 V, GND | Sensor VCC, GND | Common ground |

- [ ] Your own ranger prints a distance that changes when you move your hand
- [ ] Build and flash `firmware/phase0/0.14-ranger`. Before the loop it prints the GPIO and IO MUX registers twice: at reset and after the driver calls
- [ ] Fill in the table below from the printout, then explain each 1 by naming the call that set it

| Field | TRIG | ECHO | RED | Set by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ENABLE (output driver on) | | | | |
| FUN_IE (input path on) | | | | |
| FUN_PU, FUN_PD (pulls) | | | | |
| MCU_SEL (1 = plain GPIO on the S3) | | | | |
| out_sel, inv (what drives the pin) | | | | |

```expected
--- registers after init
TRIG  GPIO18  ENABLE=1  IN=0  mux: FUN_IE=0 FUN_PU=1 FUN_PD=0 MCU_SEL=1  out_sel=256 inv=0
echo 1166 us  199 mm
echo 1170 us  200 mm
```

Your ECHO and RED lines are the exercise. The two values above were derived from the v6.1 source and are checked by your board, not by me: `out_sel=256` is `SIG_GPIO_OUT_IDX`, “the GPIO_OUT register drives this pin”; for RED expect 73 (`LEDC_LS_SIG_OUT0_IDX`) with `inv=1`.

## How it works

**The layers.** Every ESP-IDF driver call goes down the same stack. Open each file once and you can do it for any call in the course:

| Layer | Example for `gpio_set_level` | Where in ESP-IDF v6.1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Your code | `gpio_set_level(TRIG_GPIO, 1)` | `main/main.c` |
| Driver: argument checks, locks, bookkeeping | checks the pin can output | `components/esp_driver_gpio/src/gpio.c` |
| HAL: chip-independent macro | `gpio_hal_set_level(hal, n, 1)` | `components/esp_hal_gpio/include/hal/gpio_hal.h` |
| LL (low level): one chip, `static inline` | `hw->out_w1ts = 1 << n` | `components/esp_hal_gpio/esp32s3/include/hal/gpio_ll.h` |
| Register struct and addresses | `GPIO.out_w1ts` at `GPIO_OUT_W1TS_REG` | `components/soc/esp32s3/register/soc/gpio_reg.h` |
| Silicon | the bit that drives the pad | Technical Reference Manual, “IO MUX and GPIO Matrix” |

In VS Code with PlatformIO, F12 (Go to Definition) on a call walks down this stack. The LL functions are `static inline`, so after optimisation `gpio_set_level` costs a check and one store, the same store you wrote by hand in lesson 0.13.

**Under the hood: the ranger, call by call.** Every row was read in the ESP-IDF v6.1 source.

| Call | What it does underneath | Blocks? | In an ISR? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `app_main()` | Not the start of the program. `main_task` in `freertos/app_startup.c` calls it after the scheduler is running. That task has priority 1 and a stack of `CONFIG_ESP_MAIN_TASK_STACK_SIZE` (3584 bytes by default); if `app_main` returns, the task deletes itself | n/a | n/a |
| `gpio_reset_pin(n)` | Disables the pin’s interrupt, turns the **pull-up on**, pull-down off, input and output off, releases any RTC IO use, selects the GPIO function in the IO MUX and drops the pin’s reservation | No | No |
| `gpio_set_direction(n, GPIO_MODE_OUTPUT)` | Turns the input path off (`FUN_IE` = 0), routes the plain GPIO output signal (256) through the GPIO matrix, sets the pin’s bit in `GPIO_ENABLE` through the W1TS register, selects the GPIO function, disables open-drain | No | No |
| `gpio_set_direction(n, GPIO_MODE_INPUT)` | Sets `FUN_IE` in the pin’s IO MUX register, clears its `GPIO_ENABLE` bit, selects the GPIO function | No | No |
| `gpio_set_pull_mode(n, GPIO_PULLDOWN_ONLY)` | Sets `FUN_PD` and clears `FUN_PU` in the pin’s IO MUX register: a weak internal resistor, tens of kΩ (the datasheet gives the figure) | No | No |
| `gpio_set_level(n, v)` | One store: `1 << n` into `GPIO_OUT_W1TS` (high) or `GPIO_OUT_W1TC` (low). Pins 32 and up use the `OUT1` pair | No | Yes |
| `gpio_get_level(n)` | One load: bit n of `GPIO_IN`. With the input path off, as on an output-only pin, it reads 0 | No | Yes |
| `esp_rom_delay_us(us)` | Linked to `ets_delay_us`, a routine in the chip’s mask ROM (`esp32s3.rom.api.ld`). It spins on the CPU’s cycle count, so it depends on the CPU-frequency value being current. Interrupts stay on: an interrupt during the wait makes it longer, never shorter | Spins | Yes |
| `esp_timer_get_time()` | Asks the SYSTIMER peripheral to snapshot its 64-bit counter, waits for “value valid”, reads the low half, the high half and the low half again until they agree, then divides by 16: the S3’s SYSTIMER runs at 16 MHz (40 MHz crystal ÷ 2.5). Placed in IRAM | No | Yes |
| `ledc_timer_config(&t)` | With `LEDC_AUTO_CLK`, tries the APB, XTAL and RC_FAST clocks in turn and keeps the first that can make the frequency; computes a divider with 8 fractional bits and writes it to the timer. 80 MHz ÷ (5 kHz × 256 steps) = 62.5 | No | No |
| `ledc_channel_config(&c)` | Reserves the pin (logs a warning if something else already has it), routes the LEDC channel’s output signal through the GPIO matrix to the pin, with `output_invert` applied **in the matrix**, then sets the initial duty | No | No |
| `ledc_set_duty(m, ch, d)` | In a critical section, writes `d << 4` to the channel’s duty register (the low 4 bits are a fraction). The output does **not** change yet | No | No |
| `ledc_update_duty(m, ch)` | Sets `duty_start` and the low-speed `update` bit, so the new duty is latched at the start of the next PWM period | No | Yes |
| `vTaskDelay(t)` | Moves the task to the delayed list for t ticks and yields. `vTaskDelay(0)` is only a yield | Yes | No |
| `pdMS_TO_TICKS(ms)` | A macro, not a function: `ms * configTICK_RATE_HZ / 1000` in integer arithmetic. At the default 100 Hz, 60 ms is 6 ticks and 5 ms is 0 | n/a | n/a |
| `ESP_ERROR_CHECK(x)` | Evaluates x; on anything but `ESP_OK` prints the error name, file, line and expression, then aborts. If assertions are disabled in menuconfig (`NDEBUG`), it evaluates x and **checks nothing** | n/a | n/a |
| `printf(...)` | The C library formats into stdout’s buffer; a newline (stdout is line-buffered) pushes the line to the console driver, which may wait for the host. Never inside a timing window | May wait | No |

“In an ISR? Yes” means the call takes no lock that can block. An interrupt registered with `ESP_INTR_FLAG_IRAM`, which keeps running while flash is being written, may call only code in IRAM: `esp_timer_get_time` always is; `gpio_set_level` and `gpio_get_level` only with `CONFIG_GPIO_CTRL_FUNC_IN_IRAM`; `ledc_update_duty` only with `CONFIG_LEDC_CTRL_FUNC_IN_IRAM`. Both options are off by default. Lesson 2.2 returns to this.

**What the table tells you about the ranger.**

- Measuring with `esp_timer_get_time()` in a polling loop gives 1 µs steps, but any interrupt or higher-priority task that runs between the edge and your next `gpio_get_level` adds its time to the reading. At 58 µs per centimetre a 20 µs interruption is 3 mm. Lesson 2.5 latches the edge in hardware instead.
- Three `ledc_set_duty` and `ledc_update_duty` pairs change the colour one channel at a time. Each takes effect at its channel’s next period, 200 µs at 5 kHz: invisible here, important for motor drives.
- `output_invert` costs nothing: the inversion is a wire in the GPIO matrix, not code.

## Go deeper

- [ ] Follow `esp_timer_get_time` yourself: `esp_timer/src/esp_timer_impl_systimer.c`, then `systimer_hal_get_counter_value` in `esp_hal_systimer/systimer_hal.c`, then `systimer_ll.h`. Why does it read the low half twice?
- [ ] Time `printf("x\n")` by calling `esp_timer_get_time()` before and after. Then time it without the newline. Explain the difference
- [ ] Call `gpio_get_level(TRIG_GPIO)` after setting it high. Predict the result from the table, then change the mode to `GPIO_MODE_INPUT_OUTPUT` and read it again
- [ ] Find where `ledc_set_duty_and_update` differs from the pair you used. What does it need first? (Read `ledc_fade_channel_init_check` in `esp_driver_ledc/src/ledc.c`)

## When to use it, when not to

| You need | Use | Not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| To know what a call costs or whether an ISR may call it | This table, then the source | The function name |
| A pulse width to a few microseconds, occasionally | Polling with `esp_timer_get_time` and a timeout | A loop with no timeout |
| A pulse width every time, under load | A capture peripheral (lesson 2.5) | Polling |
| A short, exact delay inside a protocol | `esp_rom_delay_us` | `vTaskDelay`, whose unit is a 10 ms tick |
| A long wait | `vTaskDelay` | `esp_rom_delay_us`, which burns the CPU |

## Break it

- [ ] Put `printf("trigger sent\n")` between the trigger pulse and the wait for the rising edge. Compare the readings with and without it at a fixed distance
- [ ] Delete `gpio_set_pull_mode` and unplug ECHO. What does the dump show for `FUN_PU`, and what does the ranger report? Which call left the pull-up on?
- [ ] Set `ch.intr_type` in the channel config, as older tutorials do. Read the compiler warning: the field is deprecated in v6.1
- [ ] Remove the divider and run from 5 V. Do not: write down instead which datasheet parameter you would be violating, and its value

## Check yourself

1. Which two registers can `gpio_set_level` write, and why is neither of them `GPIO_OUT`?
2. Why does `gpio_get_level` return 0 on a pin configured with `GPIO_MODE_OUTPUT`?
3. `ledc_set_duty` returned `ESP_OK` and the LED did not change. Why?
4. What does `ESP_ERROR_CHECK` do in a build with assertions disabled?
5. Name three calls from the table you may use inside an interrupt handler, and one you may not.

## Stretch goals

- Do the same trace for one call of your choice from lesson 2.4 or 2.5, as a table with the same four columns, and add it to your notes. Check each row in the source, not from memory
- Replace the polling with a GPIO interrupt on both edges, as in lesson 2.5 version A, and compare the spread of 100 readings at a fixed distance
- Port the ranger to plain registers for the GPIO part, using only `REG_WRITE` and `REG_READ`, and keep LEDC on the driver

## Reading

- ESP-IDF v6.1 source: `components/esp_driver_gpio/src/gpio.c`, `components/esp_hal_gpio/esp32s3/include/hal/gpio_ll.h`, `components/esp_driver_ledc/src/ledc.c`, `components/esp_timer/src/esp_timer_impl_systimer.c`
- ESP-IDF Programming Guide: “Hardware Abstraction”, which describes the driver, HAL and LL layers
- ESP32-S3 Technical Reference Manual: “IO MUX and GPIO Matrix”, “LED PWM Controller”, “System Timer”

## Common mistakes and interview angles

- **A print inside a measurement.** Formatting and output take time the measurement then includes.
- **A pin reads 0 although it is driven high.** Output-only pins have their input path off.
- **Trusting `ESP_ERROR_CHECK` to protect a release build.** It can be compiled out. Handle errors you expect.
- **Unused helper functions.** A `static` function that is never called is a warning, and with warnings as errors a failed build. Delete it or use it.
- **C++ files.** In `main.cpp`, `app_main` needs `extern "C"` so the startup code can find it; in a `.c` file it does not, and `<cstdint>` becomes `<stdint.h>`.
- **Interview angle.** “What happens when you call `gpio_set_level`?” Walk the layers: argument check, HAL macro, LL inline function, one store to the write-1-to-set register, and why that register exists (no read-modify-write race).

0.2.body:
## Why this matters

On a team, nobody asks whether you can write a blink. They ask you to check out a repository, build it and tell them why the binary grew by 40 KB. The build system is the first tool of the job.

## Prerequisites, hardware, time

Lesson 0.1 done. One S3 board. 45 minutes.

## Build it first

You will change one configuration option and measure what it does to the binary.

- [ ] In `firmware/phase0/0.1-hello`, run `idf.py size` and write down the total image size
- [ ] Run `idf.py menuconfig`, open **Compiler options**, and change **Optimization Level** to “Optimize for size”
- [ ] Save, exit, run `idf.py build` and `idf.py size` again
- [ ] Record the difference in bytes
- [ ] Open `sdkconfig` in an editor and find the line that changed
- [ ] Run `idf.py size-components` and name the three largest components

Nothing in your C file changed, yet the binary did. That is the point.

## How it works

The steps above use `idf.py`. Under PlatformIO the same actions are `pio run -e esp32s3 -t size` and `pio run -e esp32s3 -t menuconfig`, and the generated file is `sdkconfig.esp32s3`; the [toolchain cheatsheet](#sheets-toolchains) has the full mapping. Everything below applies to both.

An ESP-IDF project is a small tree with a fixed shape:

| Path | What it is | Edit it? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CMakeLists.txt` | Declares the project and pulls in ESP-IDF’s build logic | Rarely |
| `main/` | Your application component: sources and its own `CMakeLists.txt` | Yes |
| `sdkconfig.defaults` and `sdkconfig.defaults.<target>` | The few options you chose, in version control | Yes |
| `sdkconfig` | Every option, generated from the defaults and menuconfig | No, and do not commit it |
| `build/` | Everything generated: objects, the map file, the final `.bin` | Never |
| `main/idf_component.yml` | Managed dependencies from the component registry | When you add a library |
| `platformio.ini` | Tells PlatformIO which boards to build for and that the sources are in `main/` | Only if you use PlatformIO |

The commands you will use every day:

| Command | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `idf.py set-target esp32s3` | Chooses the chip and regenerates the configuration |
| `idf.py menuconfig` | Edits configuration options interactively |
| `idf.py build` | Compiles what changed and links the image |
| `idf.py -p PORT flash monitor` | Writes the image, then shows serial output |
| `idf.py size`, `idf.py size-components` | Reports where flash and RAM went |
| `idf.py fullclean` | Deletes `build/` when the configuration is confused |

**Why two configuration files.** `sdkconfig` holds thousands of options, most of which you never chose. Committing it makes every diff noisy and ties the project to one chip. `sdkconfig.defaults` records only your decisions, and the per-target file (`.esp32s3`, `.esp32`) records the ones that differ by chip. Delete `sdkconfig`, rebuild, and it is recreated from them.

## Go deeper

- [ ] Open `build/hello.map` and search for `app_main`. Note its address and size.
- [ ] Find `CONFIG_ESPTOOLPY_FLASHSIZE` in `sdkconfig`. Which defaults file set it?
- [ ] Run `idf.py build` twice in a row and time the second run. Why is it fast?

The build is a chain: CMake generates Ninja rules, the compiler turns each `.c` into an object, the linker combines objects and libraries according to a linker script, and a final tool wraps the result in the image format the bootloader expects. Lesson 1.1 opens the map file properly.

## When to use it, when not to

| Situation | Do this |
| --- | --- |
| An option every build of this project needs | Put it in `sdkconfig.defaults` |
| An option that differs between the S3 and the classic ESP32 | Put it in `sdkconfig.defaults.<target>` |
| An experiment for the next ten minutes | `idf.py menuconfig`, and do not save it into the defaults |
| The build behaves strangely after switching targets | `idf.py fullclean`, then build |

## Break it

- [ ] Add `CONFIG_ESPTOOLPY_FLASHSIZE_32MB=y` to `sdkconfig.defaults.esp32s3`, delete `sdkconfig`, build and flash. Read what the bootloader reports about the flash size, then undo it.
- [ ] Rename `main/hello_main.c` without updating `main/CMakeLists.txt`. Read the error from top to bottom and find the first line that names the real problem.

## Check yourself

1. Which file do you commit: `sdkconfig` or `sdkconfig.defaults`? Why?
2. What does `idf.py set-target` change that `idf.py build` does not?
3. Where would you look to learn which component is using the most flash?

## Stretch goals

- Set the default log level to “Warning” and measure the size change. Log strings live in flash.
- Add a custom Kconfig option to `main/` (a file named `Kconfig.projbuild`) for the tick period, and use it in the code.

## Reading

- ESP-IDF Programming Guide: “Build System” and “Project Configuration”
- *Making Embedded Systems*, chapter 2, for why configuration belongs outside the code

## Common mistakes and interview angles

- **Editing `sdkconfig` by hand and committing it.** It will be overwritten, and reviewers will not thank you.
- **Forgetting `set-target`.** The build succeeds for the wrong chip and the flasher refuses it.
- **Interview angle.** “How do you keep debug and release builds apart?” A good answer mentions separate defaults files or build directories, and that optimisation level changes timing, which changes bugs.

0.3.body:
## Why this matters

Development boards hide the flashing circuit from you. The ESP32-CAM has none, so you do by hand what the S3 board does automatically: hold a strapping pin, reset, and talk to the ROM bootloader. Once you have done it manually, boot-mode problems on any chip stop being mysterious.

## Prerequisites, hardware, time

- One ESP32-CAM, the FTDI adapter, five jumper wires
- Lesson 0.1 for the toolchain
- 45 minutes

## Build it first

Wire it with everything unplugged from USB. Set the FTDI adapter’s voltage jumper to 3.3 V logic if it has one.

| FTDI adapter | ESP32-CAM | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GND | GND | Always first |
| 5 V (VCC) | 5V | Power the board from 5 V; the 3.3 V pin of most adapters cannot supply enough current |
| TX | U0R (GPIO3) | Crossed: transmit goes to receive |
| RX | U0T (GPIO1) | |
| | IO0 to GND | A jumper wire, only while flashing |

- [ ] Wire as in the table, with IO0 jumpered to GND
- [ ] Plug in USB, then press the board’s reset button once
- [ ] In `firmware/phase0/0.3-blink`, flash. ESP-IDF: `idf.py set-target esp32`, then `idf.py -p PORT flash`. PlatformIO: `pio run -e esp32cam -t upload`
- [ ] Remove the IO0 jumper and press reset
- [ ] Open the serial monitor (`idf.py -p PORT monitor` or `pio device monitor`) and watch the small red LED on the back

```c
/* ESP32-CAM (common AI-Thinker layout): red LED on GPIO33, lit when the pin is LOW. */
#define LED_GPIO   GPIO_NUM_33
#define LED_ON     0

void app_main(void)
{
    gpio_reset_pin(LED_GPIO);
    gpio_set_direction(LED_GPIO, GPIO_MODE_OUTPUT);
    for (int n = 0; ; n++) {
        gpio_set_level(LED_GPIO, (n & 1) ? LED_ON : !LED_ON);
        printf("led %s\n", (n & 1) ? "on" : "off");
        vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(500));
    }
}
```

```expected
led off
led on
led off
```

The same project builds for the S3 (`idf.py set-target esp32s3`), where it drives an external LED on GPIO4.

## How it works

At reset the ROM bootloader samples GPIO0. High, the default thanks to an internal pull-up, means “run the program in flash”. Low means “wait for a new program over the serial port”. The jumper is you holding that pin low.

On your S3 board a USB-serial chip does this for you: the flashing tool toggles two serial control lines (DTR and RTS) that are wired through transistors to the reset and GPIO0 pins. The ESP32-CAM leaves those two transistors out to save space, so you are the transistors.

The LED lights when the pin is **low** because it is wired from 3.3 V through a resistor to the pin: the pin sinks current instead of sourcing it. “Active low” is common and worth a line in every pin table you write.

**Under the hood.** `gpio_reset_pin` turns the pin’s pull-up on and its input and output off; `gpio_set_direction` enables the output driver and routes the plain GPIO signal through the matrix; `gpio_set_level` is one store to a set or clear register. Lesson 0.13 writes those registers by hand and lesson 0.14 traces every call; the rows are in the [under-the-hood cheatsheet](#sheets-under-the-hood).

## Go deeper

- [ ] Leave the IO0 jumper on and press reset. What does the ROM print? This is the message to recognise when a product “will not boot”.
- [ ] Measure the 5 V and 3.3 V pins with a multimeter while the board runs. Record both.
- [ ] Change `LED_GPIO` to `GPIO_NUM_4`, the white flash LED, and its polarity. Do not look into it.

## When to use it, when not to

| Board | Flashing | Choose it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ESP32-S3 dev board | Automatic over USB, with built-in debugging | Learning, and anything needing speed or many pins |
| ESP32-CAM | Manual, through an adapter | A cheap camera node once the code already works |

Develop on the S3. Port to the ESP32-CAM when the feature is done.

## Break it

- [ ] Swap TX and RX and try to flash. Record the exact error.
- [ ] Power the board from the adapter’s 3.3 V pin instead of 5 V and start Wi-Fi later in the course, or simply watch the log now for a brownout message during boot.
- [ ] Flash without the IO0 jumper. Record what the tool reports after its connection attempts.

## Check yourself

1. Which pin selects download mode, and at what moment is it read?
2. Why do TX and RX cross between the adapter and the board?
3. The LED is on when the pin is low. Draw the circuit.

## Stretch goals

- Write the blink so that `LED_ON` is never mentioned in the loop: hide polarity behind a function `led_set(bool on)`.
- Find the two-transistor auto-reset circuit in the Espressif DevKitC schematic and explain it in three sentences.

## Reading

- esptool documentation: “Boot Mode Selection” for the ESP32
- The ESP32-CAM schematic for your board, if the seller published one

## Common mistakes and interview angles

- **Brownout resets.** The camera and the radio need more current than a weak USB port or a 3.3 V adapter pin can give. Power from 5 V.
- **Silent monitor.** Some adapters hold the board in reset through DTR or RTS when the monitor opens. `idf.py monitor --help` lists an option to leave those lines alone.
- **Forgetting to remove the jumper.** The board sits in download mode and looks dead.
- **Interview angle.** “A board in the field will not boot. What do you check first?” Supply voltage under load, then the strapping pins’ levels at reset, then the ROM’s first lines.

0.4.body:
## Why this matters

Firmware engineers who cannot reason about one resistor destroy pins, blame software for hardware faults, and cannot read the schematic they are given. Three laws cover most of what you will ever need.

## Prerequisites, hardware, time

An LED, a few resistors (220 Ω, 330 Ω, 1 kΩ, 10 kΩ), a breadboard, any ESP32 board for its 3.3 V pin, and a multimeter if you have one. 60 minutes.

## Build it first

Use the lab below before touching the breadboard. Set the supply to 3.3 V and a red LED, then drag the resistor from 100 Ω to 10 kΩ and watch three things: the current, the glow, and the speed of the dots.

::widget circuit

Now predict, then check in the lab, then build:

- [ ] Predict the current for a red LED and 330 Ω at 3.3 V. Check it in the lab
- [ ] Predict it for a blue LED with the same resistor. Explain the difference
- [ ] Build the red LED circuit from the 3.3 V pin to GND. Long leg of the LED toward 3.3 V
- [ ] With a multimeter: measure the voltage across the resistor and across the LED. They should add up to the supply
- [ ] Swap in 1 kΩ, then 10 kΩ. Is the LED still visible at 10 kΩ?

## How it works

**Voltage** is the push, measured between two points. **Current** is the flow, measured through one point. **Resistance** is how hard a part resists the flow.

- **Ohm’s law:** V = I × R. One resistor, three quantities; know two and you have the third.
- **Kirchhoff’s voltage law:** around any loop, the drops add up to the supply. That is why the resistor gets “whatever the LED leaves”.
- **Kirchhoff’s current law:** what flows into a junction flows out. In a single loop the current is the same everywhere, which is what the dots show.
- **Power:** P = V × I. It becomes heat, and it comes out of your battery.

An LED is not a resistor. Below its forward voltage it barely conducts; above it, the current would rise without limit. The resistor is what sets the current, so an LED straight across a supply is a short circuit with a brief light show.

The same reasoning sizes every pin you will ever use:

```
R = (V_supply − V_forward) / I_wanted
  = (3.3 V − 1.9 V) / 0.005 A
  = 280 Ω  →  use 330 Ω, the next standard value up
```

## Go deeper

A GPIO pin is a pair of transistor switches: one to the supply, one to ground. Each has some resistance of its own, so the pin’s voltage sags as you draw more current. The datasheet’s “DC characteristics” table states how much current a pin may source and sink, and what voltage it guarantees while doing so. Find that table for the ESP32-S3 and write down two numbers: the maximum current per pin and the output-high voltage at that current. You will need them in lesson 0.6.

- [ ] With the LED circuit on a GPIO-level supply, compute the power in the resistor at 330 Ω. Is a standard quarter-watt resistor in any danger?
- [ ] Two 1 kΩ resistors in series, then in parallel: predict the total, then measure it.

## When to use it, when not to

| Load | Drive it from a pin? |
| --- | --- |
| Indicator LED at a few milliamps | Yes, with a resistor |
| Several LEDs, a buzzer, a relay coil, a motor | No. Use a transistor or a driver; the pin only switches the transistor |
| Another chip’s logic input | Yes: inputs draw almost nothing |

## Break it

In the lab only, not on your board:

- [ ] Drop the resistor to its minimum at 5 V. Read the warning and the power figures.
- [ ] Set a blue LED at 3.3 V and explain to yourself why adding a smaller resistor barely helps.

## Check yourself

1. A resistor drops 1.4 V at 5 mA. What is its value?
2. Why is the current the same before and after the LED?
3. Which wastes more battery over a day: a 5 mA LED, or a sleeping ESP32 drawing 10 µA?

## Stretch goals

- Measure your LED’s real forward voltage at three currents and compare with the lab’s fixed value.
- Use the calculators’ “LED resistor” tab to choose values for 2 mA from 5 V for each LED colour.

## Reading

- *Make: Electronics*, experiments on LEDs and resistors
- The “DC Characteristics” table in the ESP32-S3 Series Datasheet

## Common mistakes and interview angles

- **LED without a resistor.** Works for a while, then the pin or the LED fails.
- **Measuring current across a part.** A multimeter in current mode is nearly a short circuit. It goes in series, in the loop.
- **Interview angle.** “Size a resistor for an LED on a 3.3 V GPIO” is asked to see whether you subtract the forward voltage and mention the pin’s current limit.

## Why this matters

“My button triggers by itself” and “the sensor works on my desk but not in the enclosure” are the same fault: a pin that nothing is holding. The other fault this lesson prevents is quieter and permanent: 5 V on a 3.3 V input.

## Prerequisites, hardware, time

A push button, your resistor kit, the HC-SR04, an S3 board. Lesson 0.4. 75 minutes.

## Build it first

Start in the lab. Leave the pin floating and watch the read value change with nothing touching it. Then add a pull-up and press the button.

::widget pin

Now on the board, with a button between GPIO5 and GND and nothing else:

- [ ] Build `firmware/phase0/0.5-pin` with `PULL_MODE 0` (floating) and flash it
- [ ] Watch the change counter for a minute. Wave your hand near the wire
- [ ] Set `PULL_MODE 1` (internal pull-up), rebuild, flash. Press the button a few times
- [ ] Record both runs’ counts side by side

```c
gpio_config_t cfg = {
    .pin_bit_mask = 1ULL << BUTTON_GPIO,
    .mode = GPIO_MODE_INPUT,
    .pull_up_en = (PULL_MODE == 1) ? GPIO_PULLUP_ENABLE : GPIO_PULLUP_DISABLE,
    .pull_down_en = (PULL_MODE == 2) ? GPIO_PULLDOWN_ENABLE : GPIO_PULLDOWN_DISABLE,
    .intr_type = GPIO_INTR_DISABLE,
};
gpio_config(&cfg);
```

With the pull-up, an untouched button gives:

```expected
level=1 changes=0
level=1 changes=0
```

## How it works

A digital input does not measure “on” or “off”. It compares a voltage with two thresholds. Above the upper one it reads 1, below the lower one it reads 0, and in between the result is not defined. An unconnected pin has almost infinite resistance, so the tiniest stray current moves its voltage anywhere.

A **pull-up** is a resistor from the pin to the supply. It is weak enough that a button to ground easily overpowers it, and strong enough that stray currents do not. A **pull-down** is the mirror image. The chip has both built in, at tens of kilohms; you enable them in software.

**Logic levels.** Your ESP32 is a 3.3 V device: its pins are not built to tolerate 5 V. The HC-SR04 is powered from 5 V and drives its ECHO pin to 5 V. Two resistors fix that:

::widget calc

With 1 kΩ on top and 2 kΩ on the bottom, 5 V becomes 3.33 V. In the other direction no divider is needed: the 3.3 V the ESP32 sends to TRIG is above the sensor’s threshold for a 1.

This is what that echo pin is telling you, and why its timing is the whole measurement:

::widget echo

**Decoupling and ground.** Every chip draws current in sharp bursts. A 100 nF capacitor next to its supply pin delivers those bursts locally so they do not appear as noise on the rail. And every signal is a voltage measured against ground, so two boards that talk must share a ground wire. Half of all “random” bus errors are a missing ground.

## Go deeper

- [ ] Compute the current through a 10 kΩ pull-up when the button is pressed at 3.3 V. Then for 100 Ω. Why not use 100 Ω?
- [ ] The internal pull-up is weak. Predict what happens to a pulled-up pin at the end of a two-metre wire next to a motor.
- [ ] Find the input threshold voltages in the ESP32-S3 datasheet’s DC characteristics table and compare them with the lab’s dashed lines.

## When to use it, when not to

| Situation | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Button or switch on a short wire | Internal pull-up, button to ground |
| Long wires, noisy surroundings | External pull-up of 1 kΩ to 10 kΩ, plus a small capacitor |
| I2C lines | External pull-ups always; the internal ones are too weak for the bus speed |
| 5 V output into a 3.3 V input, slow signal | Resistor divider |
| 5 V signals in both directions, or fast | Level-shifter module |

## Break it

- [ ] Configure the pin as an input with a pull-up, but wire the button to 3.3 V instead of ground. Predict the readings before you flash.
- [ ] In the divider calculator, swap R1 and R2. What voltage would the ESP32 pin see?

## Check yourself

1. Why does a floating input sometimes read correctly for hours?
2. With a pull-up, what level means “pressed”?
3. Why is a divider fine for ECHO but not for powering a 3.3 V sensor from 5 V?

## Stretch goals

- Wire the HC-SR04 with the divider and look at ECHO on the logic analyzer when it arrives. Compare the pulse width with the echo lab for a measured distance.
- Add a 100 nF capacitor from the button pin to ground and repeat the floating test.

## Reading

- *Make: Electronics*, the sections on switches and pull-up resistors
- ESP-IDF Programming Guide: “GPIO & RTC GPIO”

## Common mistakes and interview angles

- **Relying on a pull that is not there.** Some pins have no internal pull resistors; check before relying on one.
- **Forgetting the shared ground.** Two boards, two USB ports, no ground wire between them.
- **Interview angle.** “What is a pull-up for, and how do you choose its value?” Mention defined idle level, the current when driven low, and rise time on a capacitive line.

0.6.body:
## Why this matters

The datasheet is the contract and the schematic is the map. Tutorials are someone’s memory of both. The engineers who are trusted with hardware are the ones who go to the source, and it is a learnable skill: you are looking for about six tables.

## Prerequisites, hardware, time

Your S3 board and a notebook or spreadsheet. The ESP32-S3 Series Datasheet, the ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 user guide, and the MPU6050 datasheet, all free from the manufacturers. 90 minutes.

## Build it first

You are building the one document you will open in every later lesson: your own pin table. Your board is probably a clone, so the silkscreen on it outranks any diagram online.

- [ ] List every pin label printed on your board, in order, both sides
- [ ] Mark the pins the module uses for flash and PSRAM. On N16R8 that includes GPIO35, 36 and 37
- [ ] Mark the two USB pins, GPIO19 and GPIO20
- [ ] Mark the four strapping pins. Find them in the datasheet section named “Strapping Pins”
- [ ] Mark the UART0 pins used by the USB-serial bridge
- [ ] Find which pin drives the on-board RGB LED. It is printed on some boards; otherwise it is GPIO48 or GPIO38
- [ ] Choose eight “safe first choice” pins and highlight them

Compare your table with the course’s [pin warnings cheatsheet](#sheets-s3-pins). Where they differ, your board wins; note the difference.

::widget chip

## How it works

**What a datasheet contains, in the order you will use it.**

| Section | Answers | You used or will use it in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Features, block diagram | What is this part, in one page | 0.1 |
| Pin description | What each pin can do; which have special roles at reset | This lesson |
| Absolute maximum ratings | What destroys it | 0.5 |
| Recommended operating conditions | What it is guaranteed to work at | Every power decision |
| DC characteristics | Thresholds, drive current, leakage | 0.4, 0.5 |
| Timing diagrams and tables | How fast, and in what order | All of Phase 3 |
| Register map | Every bit you can read or write | 0.13, and every driver you write |

Absolute maximum is not a target. A part run at its absolute maximum is being damaged slowly. Design to the recommended conditions.

**What a schematic contains.** Symbols for parts, lines for wires, and names on wires: two wires with the same net name are connected even when no line joins them. Power symbols (3V3, GND) are net names too. Read a schematic by following one signal from the connector to the chip and naming every part it touches.

**The chip has more than one document.** The datasheet covers electrical facts and pins. The Technical Reference Manual covers how each peripheral works and its registers. The module datasheet covers the metal can on your board: which flash, which PSRAM, which pins those consume. The errata lists the bugs in the silicon. Knowing which document answers which question is half the skill.

## Go deeper

Answer each from the source and write down the page number. The page number is the point: it is how you will cite a fact in a design review.

- [ ] MPU6050: what is its I2C address, and which pin changes it?
- [ ] MPU6050: what supply voltage range does it accept? Is it safe on 3.3 V?
- [ ] MPU6050: which register do you read to confirm you are talking to the right chip, and what value should it return?
- [ ] ESP32-S3: what is the absolute maximum voltage on an input pin?
- [ ] DevKitC-1 schematic: follow the BOOT button. Which pin does it pull, and to what?

## When to use it, when not to

| You want | Open |
| --- | --- |
| A pin’s electrical limits | Chip datasheet |
| How to configure a timer or what a register bit does | Technical Reference Manual |
| Which pins the memory uses on your module | Module datasheet |
| Why a documented feature misbehaves | Errata |
| A quick wiring picture | A tutorial, then verify it against the above |

## Break it

- [ ] Find a pinout diagram for “ESP32-S3 N16R8” from an image search and compare it with your table. List every disagreement. There is usually at least one.

## Check yourself

1. Two wires on a schematic do not touch but share a name. Are they connected?
2. What is the difference between “absolute maximum” and “recommended operating” voltage?
3. Which document tells you what bit 3 of a control register does?

## Stretch goals

- Do the same six-table tour for the HC-SR04 and the SSD1306. Note what is missing from the cheaper part’s documentation.
- Draw the schematic of your lesson 0.4 circuit by hand, with net names.

## Reading

- ESP32-S3 Series Datasheet: pin description and electrical characteristics
- *Making Embedded Systems*, the chapter on reading datasheets and schematics

## Common mistakes and interview angles

- **Trusting a diagram for a different board revision.** The LED pin moved between DevKitC-1 revisions; clones vary more.
- **Reading “typical” as “guaranteed”.** Design to the minimum and maximum columns.
- **Interview angle.** You may be handed a datasheet and asked for one number. Being quick and saying where you found it is the whole test.

## Why this matters

Digital signals are analog signals that we agree to read at the right moment. Every “impossible” bug on a wire, the double-counted button or the byte that arrives wrong once a day, lives in the gap between that agreement and the real voltage.

## Prerequisites, hardware, time

A push button, an S3 board, and the logic analyzer if it has arrived (the lab stands in for it until then). Lesson 0.5. 75 minutes.

## Build it first

Press the switch in the lab a few times. Set the debounce window to zero and count how many presses an interrupt would see. Then find the shortest window that always gives exactly one.

::widget bounce

Now measure a real one. Button between GPIO5 and GND:

- [ ] Build and flash `firmware/phase0/0.7-bounce`. It counts falling edges with an interrupt
- [ ] Press the button ten times, deliberately. Record the count
- [ ] If you have the logic analyzer: capture one press at 1 MHz or faster and measure how long the bouncing lasts
- [ ] Try a different button or a bare jumper wire touched to ground. Compare

```c
static volatile uint32_t edges;

static void IRAM_ATTR on_edge(void *arg)
{
    edges++;
}
```

Ten clean presses would print 10. A real button typically gives more:

```expected
edges=1
edges=4
edges=5
edges=9
```

Your numbers will differ; that they are not 1, 2, 3 is the result.

## How it works

**Thresholds.** A wire carries a voltage; the input turns it into 0 or 1 by comparing it with thresholds, as you saw in lesson 0.5. Between them the reading is undefined.

**Edges.** The transition from one level to the other is an edge: rising or falling. Edges are where information and trouble both live. An interrupt “on the falling edge” fires every time the signal crosses downward, however briefly.

**Rise time.** No edge is instant. The wire has capacitance, and whatever drives it has resistance, so the voltage curves toward its new level. A slow edge spends longer in the undefined band. That is why a weak pull-up on a long wire causes errors at speed, and why I2C has a maximum bus capacitance.

**Bounce.** Two pieces of metal closing do not close once. They make and break contact for a few milliseconds, and each one is a perfectly valid edge. The button is not faulty; your assumption was.

**Debouncing.** Accept a new level only after it has held steady for a set time. The cost is latency, as the lab shows. Two other approaches exist and you will meet both: sample the pin on a slow timer instead of using an edge interrupt, or filter in hardware with a resistor and capacitor.

**Glitches.** A glitch is a pulse shorter than anything intended: crosstalk from a neighbouring wire, a spike when a motor switches. You cannot see one by printing. You see it with an instrument that samples much faster than the signal, which is what the logic analyzer is for.

## Go deeper

- [ ] Your analyzer samples at 24 MHz at most. What is the shortest pulse it can reliably show? What would a 10 ns glitch look like in a capture?
- [ ] In the lab, set bounce to 8 ms and the window to 5 ms. Explain the result, then fix it.
- [ ] The interrupt handler has `IRAM_ATTR` and the counter is `volatile`. Write one sentence guessing why for each; lessons 1.3 and 2.2 will confirm or correct you.

## When to use it, when not to

| Input | Approach |
| --- | --- |
| Human button | Debounce in software, 5 to 20 ms; latency is invisible to a person |
| Rotary encoder, fast | Hardware filter or a peripheral with a glitch filter (lesson 2.8) |
| Signal from another chip | No debounce: it does not bounce. If it glitches, fix the wiring |
| Limit switch on a machine | Debounce, and think about what a missed edge costs |

## Break it

- [ ] Change the interrupt to trigger on any edge and predict the new count for ten presses before you try it.
- [ ] Remove the pull-up configuration from the 0.7 project and explain the count you get with the button untouched.

## Check yourself

The Phase 0 quiz has a waveform to decode. Before it:

1. Why does a slow edge cause more errors than a fast one?
2. What does debouncing cost?
3. Why can a serial print not show you a glitch?

## Stretch goals

- Write the debounce yourself in the 0.7 project: a 1 ms periodic check that accepts a level after five identical samples.
- Capture the bounce of three different switches and put the screenshots in your signal notebook.

## Reading

- “A Guide to Debouncing” by Jack Ganssle, a classic measured study, free online
- *Making Embedded Systems*, the section on buttons and inputs

## Common mistakes and interview angles

- **Debouncing with a delay inside the interrupt handler.** It blocks everything else. Record a timestamp and decide later.
- **Assuming all switches bounce alike.** They range from under a millisecond to tens.
- **Interview angle.** “Debounce a button” is a standard whiteboard task. Say what you are trading (latency for certainty), then give a timer-based version.

0.8.body:
## Why this matters

Every sensor reading, every audio sample and every input to a neural network in Phase 9 is a continuous signal turned into numbers. Do it too slowly and the numbers describe a signal that never existed, with nothing in the data to warn you.

## Prerequisites, hardware, time

An S3 board and one jumper wire. Lessons 0.5 and 0.7. 75 minutes.

## Build it first

In the lab, leave the sample rate at 80 Hz and drag the signal frequency upward. Watch what the dots do as you pass 40 Hz.

::widget sampling

Then make your board lie to itself. The firmware generates a 100 Hz square wave on GPIO6 and samples it with the ADC on GPIO4:

- [ ] Wire GPIO6 to GPIO4 with one jumper
- [ ] Build and flash `firmware/phase0/0.8-adc` with `SAMPLE_HZ 2000`. The output shows runs of ten high, ten low
- [ ] Set `SAMPLE_HZ 110`. One cycle now seems to take eleven samples: your 100 Hz wave is posing as 10 Hz
- [ ] Set `SAMPLE_HZ 100`. Explain what you see before reading on

```c
adc_oneshot_unit_init_cfg_t unit_cfg = { .unit_id = unit };
adc_oneshot_new_unit(&unit_cfg, &adc);
adc_oneshot_chan_cfg_t chan_cfg = { .bitwidth = ADC_BITWIDTH_DEFAULT, .atten = ADC_ATTEN_DB_12 };
adc_oneshot_config_channel(adc, channel, &chan_cfg);
/* ... once per sample period ... */
adc_oneshot_read(adc, channel, &raw);
```

At 2000 samples per second the square wave is obvious; values vary a little:

```expected
4095
4095
4095
0
0
0
```

At exactly 100 samples per second, every sample lands on the same point of the wave and the output is a constant. A 100 Hz signal has become DC.

## How it works

**Sampling** reads the signal at regular instants and discards everything between them.

**The Nyquist limit.** To recover a frequency you need more than two samples per cycle. So a sample rate *fs* can represent frequencies up to *fs*/2 and nothing above.

**Aliasing.** A frequency above *fs*/2 does not vanish. It folds back and appears as a lower one: a tone at *f* sampled at *fs* shows up at the distance between *f* and the nearest multiple of *fs*. The lab’s dashed line passes through every sample exactly, which is the uncomfortable part: no amount of software can tell the two apart afterwards. The only defence is a filter *before* the converter that removes what you cannot represent.

See the same thing in the frequency domain. Push a tone above half the sample rate and watch where its peak lands:

::widget fft

**Quantization.** The converter also rounds each sample to one of 2^bits levels. A 12-bit ADC over a 3.3 V range has steps of about 0.8 mV. Drag the resolution down in the sampling lab to see the staircase. The rounding error behaves like added noise, about half a step in size.

**Resolution is not accuracy.** Twelve bits of resolution with 20 mV of noise on the supply is not twelve useful bits. Averaging several samples trades speed for a quieter number; calibration fixes offset and gain. Lesson 2.6 measures both on your board.

## Go deeper

- [ ] A sensor’s signal contains nothing above 50 Hz, but the mains adds 50 Hz hum and its harmonics. What sample rate would you choose, and what would you put in front of the ADC?
- [ ] You sample a 1 kHz tone at 1.1 kHz. At what frequency does it appear? Check with the lab’s arithmetic.
- [ ] The firmware samples from a hardware timer, not a delay loop. What would jitter in the sample instants do to the readings? Lesson 0.9 answers it.

## When to use it, when not to

| Signal | Sample at | Because |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Room temperature | Once a second or slower | It cannot change faster |
| Accelerometer for gestures | 50 to 200 Hz | Human motion is mostly below 20 Hz |
| Vibration of a motor | Several kHz | Faults show up as high harmonics |
| Speech | 16 kHz | Intelligibility needs up to about 7 kHz |

Sample as slowly as the signal allows: every extra sample costs power, memory and processing.

## Break it

- [ ] In the FFT viewer set the sample rate to 1000 Hz and tone 2 to 900 Hz. Where does the peak appear? Now explain why a microphone circuit has a low-pass filter in it.

## Check yourself

1. What is the highest frequency a 16 kHz sample rate can represent?
2. A 70 Hz signal is sampled at 100 Hz. What frequency do the samples show?
3. Why can aliasing not be removed after sampling?

## Stretch goals

- Print the samples as CSV, plot them in Python, and overlay the true 100 Hz wave.
- Average 16 readings per sample and compare the spread of the values.

## Reading

- ESP-IDF Programming Guide: “Analog to Digital Converter (ADC) Oneshot Mode Driver”
- *Making Embedded Systems*, the chapter on doing more with less (sampling and filtering)

## Common mistakes and interview angles

- **Sampling “fast enough” by feel.** Compute the highest frequency present, including noise.
- **Trusting the last bits of an ADC reading.** Look at the spread of repeated readings first.
- **Interview angle.** “What is aliasing and how do you prevent it?” The complete answer includes the analog filter before the ADC, not only the sample rate.
