## Why this matters
Knowing the primitives is not design. This lesson is about deciding which tasks exist, what they own and how they talk, before writing them.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lessons 4.1 to 4.10. 3 hours, mostly on paper.
## Build it first
::widget pid

- [ ] For the capstone, list every activity with its period, worst-case time and deadline
- [ ] Group activities into tasks. Draw each task as a box, each queue as an arrow, and write who owns each peripheral
- [ ] Assign priorities by deadline and compute total CPU use
- [ ] Mark every blocking call and its timeout
- [ ] In the PID lab, find gains that work; then note the loop rate your design must guarantee for them to hold
## How it works
**One owner per resource.** The display belongs to the display task; others send it messages. Ownership removes most locks.

**Pipelines.** Sensor task, then processing, then output, joined by queues. Each stage has one job and can be tested alone.

**Active objects.** A task with a private state machine and an inbox queue; it does nothing except react to messages. No shared state, so no races by construction.

**Rate-monotonic priority.** Among periodic tasks, the shorter the period, the higher the priority. If total utilisation stays under about 70%, deadlines are met; above that you must analyse.

Write the timing budget down. A design you cannot draw on one page has too many interactions.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Where in your design could a slow consumer stall a producer? Is that what you want?
## When to use it, when not to
| Pattern | Fits |
| --- | --- |
| Pipeline | Data flowing one way |
| Active object | Stateful components reacting to events |
| Shared data with a mutex | Rarely changing configuration |
## Break it
- [ ] Find the one queue in your design whose overflow would be silent, and decide what should happen instead.
## Check yourself
1. Why does single ownership reduce locking?
2. What is rate-monotonic priority assignment?
3. What belongs in a timing budget?
## Stretch goals
- Review an open-source ESP-IDF project’s task structure against these ideas.
## Reading
*Making Embedded Systems*, the architecture chapters.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **One task per function.** Tasks are for independent timing, not for tidiness.
- **Interview angle.** “Design the task architecture for a battery-powered sensor node.”

## Why this matters
Zephyr appears in a growing share of postings. A few hours with it shows that tasks, queues and drivers are concepts, not FreeRTOS features, and introduces devicetree before Phase 8.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
An S3 board; the Zephyr SDK and its `west` tool. 5 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Install Zephyr and build its blinky sample for your board; the exact board name is in Zephyr’s board list
- [ ] Find the LED’s pin: it is not in the C file. Open the board’s devicetree and locate it
- [ ] Add an overlay that declares the MPU6050 on the I2C bus, enable its driver in the project configuration, and read acceleration through the generic sensor interface
- [ ] Create a second thread and a message queue; pass readings between them
## How it works
Zephyr is an RTOS with its own build system and a large driver collection, used across many vendors’ chips.

**Devicetree** describes the hardware, which bus, which pins, which address, in data files instead of code. The same application builds for another board by changing the tree. Linux uses the same idea, which is why this is worth an afternoon.

**Kconfig** selects which subsystems are compiled in; you have used the same tool in ESP-IDF’s configuration menu.

| Concept | FreeRTOS | Zephyr |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Task | `xTaskCreate` | `k_thread` |
| Queue | `xQueueSend` | `k_msgq_put` |
| Mutex | `xSemaphoreTake` | `k_mutex_lock` |
| Delay | `vTaskDelay` | `k_sleep` |
## Go deeper

## When to use it, when not to
| Choose | When |
| --- | --- |
| ESP-IDF | Espressif chips, full use of their radios and peripherals |
| Zephyr | One codebase across several vendors; teams standardised on it |

2. What is the Zephyr equivalent of a FreeRTOS queue?

## Why this matters
Edge AI is the destination. Seeing a model run on your board now, months before Phase 9, shows what all this plumbing is for and starts the dataset you will need.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
An S3 board and the MPU6050. Lessons 3.2 and 4.4. 3 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Add the TensorFlow Lite Micro component and build its smallest example, a model that approximates a sine wave
- [ ] Time the `Invoke()` call with a microsecond timer. Print the tensor arena size it needed
- [ ] Read the code: find the model array, the interpreter, the arena, the input and output tensors
- [ ] Separately, write a logger: IMU at 100 Hz through a queue to the serial port as CSV
- [ ] Record three gestures, twenty repetitions each, into labelled files. Keep them: lesson 9.1 trains on them
## How it works
A model on a microcontroller is an array of bytes in flash plus an interpreter that walks it. All working memory comes from one static block, the **tensor arena**; nothing is allocated while it runs. You copy numbers into an input tensor, call invoke, and read an output tensor.

The data pipeline around it is everything you have built: a sensor driver, a periodic task, a queue, a buffer. Phase 9 replaces the sine model with one trained on the data you are recording now.
## Go deeper

## Why this matters
A connected product spends most of its life reconnecting. The happy path is ten lines; the engineering is what happens when the router reboots at 3 a.m.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
An S3 board and a Wi-Fi network you control. Lessons 4.6 and 2.10. 4 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Connect as a station using the event loop: handle “started”, “disconnected” and “got IP” as events, never as a delay loop
- [ ] Track state in an event group so other tasks can wait for “connected”
- [ ] Unplug the router for a minute. Reconnect with exponential back-off, capped, with a little randomness
- [ ] Print the disconnect reason each time; try a wrong password
- [ ] Start an access point and connect your phone to it
- [ ] Measure current during connection with your power meter
## How it works
Wi-Fi runs in its own high-priority task and tells you what happened through **events**. Connecting is asynchronous: you ask, and later an event says it worked or why it failed.

**Station** mode joins a network; **access point** mode creates one, usually just for set-up. Getting an address by DHCP is a separate step after association, with its own event.

Retrying immediately and for ever drains batteries and hammers a recovering router. **Back-off** waits longer after each failure; **jitter** stops a hundred devices retrying in step.
## Go deeper
- [ ] What should the device do with sensor readings taken while offline?
## When to use it, when not to
| Link | Use Wi-Fi when |
| --- | --- |
| Mains power or large battery, a network exists | Yes |
| Coin cell, tiny payloads | BLE or LoRa |
## Break it
- [ ] Block inside an event handler and watch the connection stall.
## Check yourself
1. Why is connecting event-driven?
2. What are back-off and jitter for?
3. Which two steps must both succeed before you can send data?
## Stretch goals
- Scan for networks and choose the strongest of several known ones.
## Reading
ESP-IDF guide: “Wi-Fi Driver”, the event and reconnect sections.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Credentials in source control.**
- **Interview angle.** “How do you make a device’s connection robust?”

## Why this matters
A product cannot ship with your home network’s password compiled in. Provisioning is how a customer gives the device its credentials, and it is the first thing a security reviewer looks at.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lesson 5.1 and a phone. 3 hours.

The device starts with no credentials and offers a temporary, authenticated channel: BLE, or its own access point. The app sends the network name and password over an encrypted session, proven by a code printed on the device. The device stores them in NVS and connects.

Three things make it a product feature and not a demo: proof of possession so a neighbour cannot provision your device; a way back when credentials are wrong; and a deliberate reset.

## Why this matters
Every network protocol above this is a pattern of bytes on a TCP or UDP socket. Seeing those bytes in a capture is the networking equivalent of the logic analyzer.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lesson 5.1; Wireshark on your computer. 3 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Write a TCP echo server on the board; connect with `nc` and type
- [ ] Capture it in Wireshark: find the three-way handshake, your data, the acknowledgements and the close
- [ ] Send a reading every second by UDP to your computer; drop the link briefly and see what is lost
- [ ] Set a receive timeout so a silent peer does not block the task for ever
- [ ] Handle the peer disconnecting: what does `recv` return?
## How it works
**IP** delivers packets to an address, with no promises. **UDP** adds ports and nothing else: a datagram arrives whole or not at all, possibly out of order. **TCP** builds a reliable, ordered **byte stream** with acknowledgements and retransmission, at the cost of connection set-up, memory per connection and unpredictable delays when packets are lost.

TCP has no message boundaries: two sends may arrive as one receive, or one as two. Your framing from lesson 1.14 is what restores them.

The sockets API is the same one used on every operating system; here it is provided by the lwIP stack, running as a task.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Why can a TCP “send” succeed although the data never arrives?
## When to use it, when not to
| Traffic | Transport |
| --- | --- |
| Must arrive, in order | TCP |
| Latest value matters, old ones are worthless; discovery; time sync | UDP |
## Break it
- [ ] Assume one `recv` returns one whole message and send two quickly.
## Check yourself
1. What does TCP guarantee that UDP does not?
2. Why does TCP need framing on top?
3. What does a return of zero from `recv` mean?
## Stretch goals
- Serve two clients at once with `select`.
## Reading
ESP-IDF guide: “lwIP”. “Beej’s Guide to Network Programming”, free online.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **No timeouts on sockets.**
- **Interview angle.** “TCP versus UDP: when each?”

## Why this matters
Devices fetch configuration, post data and download updates over HTTPS. TLS is what makes that safe, and misconfiguring it is the commonest serious security flaw in IoT products.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lesson 5.3. 4 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Make an HTTP GET with the HTTP client and print the status and body
- [ ] Switch to HTTPS using the built-in certificate bundle
- [ ] Pin one server’s root certificate instead, embedded in the firmware
- [ ] Point the same code at a server with a different certificate. It must fail: confirm it does
- [ ] Set the clock wrong by a year and see the handshake fail; note why TLS needs time
- [ ] Measure the heap used during the handshake
## How it works
**HTTP** is text: a request line, headers, a blank line, a body; a status code comes back.

**TLS** wraps the connection. The server presents a **certificate**; the device checks that it was signed by an authority it trusts, that it names the right host and that it is in date. Then both sides agree keys and everything is encrypted.

The device’s trust comes from certificates stored in the firmware: a bundle of public authorities, or one pinned root. Skipping verification makes the encryption worthless: anyone can impersonate the server.

TLS is expensive on a microcontroller: tens of kilobytes of RAM and a second or more of handshake. Reuse connections.
## Go deeper
- [ ] The pinned certificate expires in five years and devices live for ten. What is your plan?
## When to use it, when not to
| Choice | When |
| --- | --- |
| Certificate bundle | Talking to arbitrary public servers |
| Pinned root | Your own backend |
| Plain HTTP | Never across a network you do not control |
## Break it
- [ ] Disable certificate verification “to get it working” and write down what you would have shipped.
## Check yourself
1. What does the device verify in a certificate?
2. Why does TLS need the correct time?
3. What does skipping verification allow?
## Stretch goals
- Serve a page from the device with the HTTP server component.
## Reading
ESP-IDF guide: “ESP HTTP Client” and “ESP-TLS”.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Verification switched off in production.**
- **Interview angle.** “How does TLS protect a device’s connection, and what can go wrong?”

5.5.body:
## Why this matters
MQTT is how most fleets of devices report and receive commands: small, tolerant of bad links, and decoupled through a broker.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lesson 5.4; a broker on your computer (Mosquitto). 4 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Add the MQTT client as a managed component (in ESP-IDF v6.1 it is no longer built in) and connect to your broker
- [ ] Publish temperature every ten seconds to `home/room1/temperature`; subscribe from your computer
- [ ] Subscribe on the device to `home/room1/led/set` and act on it
- [ ] Publish a retained “online” on connect and set a last-will of “offline”. Pull the power and watch the broker announce it
- [ ] Publish at QoS 0 and QoS 1 while toggling Wi-Fi; count what arrives
## How it works
Clients connect to a **broker** and never to each other. A publisher sends a message to a **topic**, a path-like name; the broker forwards it to every subscriber of that topic. Wildcards subscribe to families of topics.

**QoS 0:** sent once, may be lost. **QoS 1:** acknowledged and retried, may arrive twice. **QoS 2:** exactly once, at double the traffic.

A **retained** message is kept by the broker and given to new subscribers at once: ideal for state. The **last will** is a message the broker publishes for you if you vanish without saying goodbye.

Design topics like an API: stable, hierarchical, state separate from commands.
## Go deeper
- [ ] With QoS 1, a “toggle” command may arrive twice. How should commands be designed so that does not matter?
## When to use it, when not to
| Pattern | Protocol |
| --- | --- |
| Many devices, telemetry and commands | MQTT |
| Request and response with a server | HTTPS |
| Very constrained, UDP-only links | CoAP |
## Break it
- [ ] Connect two devices with the same client ID.
## Check yourself
1. What does the broker do?
2. What can QoS 1 do that QoS 0 cannot, and at what cost?
3. What is a last-will message for?
## Stretch goals
- Use TLS to the broker with a client certificate.
## Reading
ESP-MQTT documentation. The MQTT 3.1.1 specification’s introduction.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Commands that are not idempotent.**
- **Interview angle.** “Explain MQTT QoS levels.”

5.6.body:
## Why this matters
A device you can open in a browser on the local network needs no cloud and no app. Three small protocols make that work.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lessons 5.4 and 6.2 (or embed the page in the firmware for now). 3 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Announce the device with mDNS and open it by name from your browser
- [ ] Set the clock with SNTP and print local time with a time-zone string
- [ ] Serve a page; push live sensor values to it over a WebSocket
- [ ] Count how many browser tabs the device can serve at once
## How it works
**mDNS** answers name queries on the local network, so the device is `sensor.local` and not an address that changes.

**SNTP** fetches the time from a server. Until it has, the clock reads 1970, and TLS and timestamps are wrong.

A **WebSocket** upgrades an HTTP connection into a two-way message channel, so the device can push updates without the page polling.

**CoAP** is HTTP’s ideas (resources, GET, PUT) over UDP in a few bytes, for networks too constrained for TCP. Know that it exists.
## Go deeper
- [ ] What should the firmware do with timestamps taken before the clock was set?
## When to use it, when not to
| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Find the device by name locally | mDNS |
| Live updates in a browser | WebSocket |
| Correct time | SNTP, plus an RTC to survive outages |
## Break it
- [ ] Open twenty connections and watch the heap.
## Check yourself
1. What problem does mDNS solve?
2. Why does a device need the time?
3. How does a WebSocket differ from repeated HTTP requests?
## Stretch goals
- Add a settings form that writes to NVS.
## Reading
ESP-IDF guide: “HTTP Server”, “mDNS Service”, “System Time”.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Unbounded connections.** Each costs RAM.
- **Interview angle.** “How would a user configure a headless device locally?”

5.7.body:
## Why this matters
Bluetooth Low Energy is how a device talks to a phone, and how battery devices communicate at all. Its model, attributes instead of streams, is different from everything so far.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
An S3 board and a phone with a BLE scanner app. 5 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Start from the NimBLE peripheral example for your version. Advertise with your own device name and find it from the phone
- [ ] Define a service with two characteristics: temperature (read and notify) and LED (write)
- [ ] Read, subscribe and write from the phone app
- [ ] Capture the advertising data’s raw bytes and decode the length-type-value records
- [ ] Require pairing before the LED characteristic can be written
- [ ] Measure current while advertising at 100 ms and at 1 s intervals
## How it works
A **peripheral** advertises: short broadcasts saying “I exist, this is what I am”. A **central**, usually a phone, scans and connects.

Once connected, data is exposed as **GATT**: a table of **characteristics** grouped into **services**, each with a UUID and permissions. The central reads and writes them; the peripheral can **notify** when one changes. There is no stream: everything is a small named value.

**Pairing** establishes keys; **bonding** stores them. Without it, anyone in range can read and write.

Power is governed by intervals: how often you advertise, and how often a connection wakes. The S3 has BLE only, no Bluetooth Classic.
## Go deeper
- [ ] A characteristic holds at most a few hundred bytes. How would you transfer a 100 KB file?
## When to use it, when not to
| Link | Use BLE when |
| --- | --- |
| Phone is the user interface | Yes |
| Years on a coin cell | Yes |
| Megabytes, or internet without a phone | Wi-Fi |
## Break it
- [ ] Leave the write characteristic open and change the LED from a stranger’s phone app.
## Check yourself
1. What is the difference between advertising and a connection?
2. What is a characteristic?
3. What do pairing and bonding provide?
## Stretch goals
- Implement the standard Environmental Sensing service so generic apps understand your device.
## Reading
ESP-IDF guide: “NimBLE-based host APIs”. Bluetooth SIG’s GATT overview.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Treating BLE as a serial cable.**
- **Interview angle.** “Explain GATT: services, characteristics, notifications.”

## Why this matters
Sometimes two devices only need to talk to each other, instantly, with no router. ESP-NOW does that in a few lines and a few milliseconds.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Two ESP32 boards. Lesson 5.1. 2 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Send a struct from one board to the other by MAC address; print it on arrival
- [ ] Use the send callback to learn whether the peer acknowledged
- [ ] Measure the time from button press on one to LED on the other
- [ ] Walk away until packets drop; note the range
- [ ] Enable encryption between the pair
## How it works
ESP-NOW sends small frames directly between Espressif chips over the Wi-Fi radio, with no access point, no IP and no connection set-up. Frames are addressed by MAC and may be acknowledged at the link layer.

It is fast and simple, and it is not a network: no routing, a small payload, a limited number of encrypted peers, and both ends must be on the same channel. It is proprietary to Espressif chips.
## Go deeper
- [ ] How would a sleeping sensor and an always-on hub use ESP-NOW to minimise the sensor’s awake time?
## When to use it, when not to
| Use it for | Not for |
| --- | --- |
| Remote controls, sensor to hub, wireless serial cable | Internet access, other vendors’ devices, large data |
## Break it
- [ ] Put the two boards on different Wi-Fi channels.
## Check yourself
1. What does ESP-NOW not need that Wi-Fi does?
2. How is a peer addressed?
3. Name two limits.
## Stretch goals
- Build a hub that forwards ESP-NOW readings to MQTT.
## Reading
ESP-IDF guide: “ESP-NOW”.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Forgetting the channel must match the access point’s when the hub also uses Wi-Fi.**
- **Interview angle.** Compare the links you have used by power, range and data rate.

5.9.body:
## Why this matters
Lesson 2.13 explained safe updates. Now you ship one: over HTTPS, with a self-test, and a deliberately bad image to prove the rollback works.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lessons 2.13 and 5.4; a file server on your computer. 4 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Switch to a two-slot partition table and enable rollback in the bootloader configuration
- [ ] Serve version 2 of your firmware over HTTPS; have version 1 download and install it with the HTTPS OTA component
- [ ] On first boot of a new image, run a self-test (Wi-Fi connects, sensor answers); only then mark the image valid
- [ ] Build a version 3 that crashes after five seconds. Install it and watch the device return to version 2
- [ ] Cut power in the middle of a download. Confirm the old image still runs
- [ ] Print the running version and partition at boot
## How it works
The update is written to the inactive slot while the active one runs. After verification, the boot record is switched and the device restarts.

With **rollback** enabled, a new image boots in a pending state. Your code must call the “mark valid” function once it has proved itself. If the device resets first, the bootloader reverts.

The self-test is the design decision: it should prove the device can do the one thing that lets you update it again.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Who is allowed to tell the device to update, and how does the device know the image is yours? Lesson 5.10 continues.
## When to use it, when not to
| Fleet | Strategy |
| --- | --- |
| A few devices | Manual trigger |
| Many | Staged rollout: 1%, then 10%, then all, watching telemetry |
## Break it
- [ ] Mark the image valid as the first line of `app_main`, then install the crashing build.
## Check yourself
1. When should an image be marked valid?
2. What happens to a pending image that resets?
3. What should the self-test prove?
## Stretch goals
- Report the result of each update over MQTT.
## Reading
ESP-IDF guide: “Over The Air Updates (OTA)” and “ESP HTTPS OTA”.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **An update that breaks the updater.**
- **Interview angle.** “Describe an OTA system you would trust in the field.”

5.10.body:
## Why this matters
A connected device is a computer on someone’s network, physically in an attacker’s hands. Security is a set of specific mechanisms answering specific threats, and several are irreversible.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
One S3 board you are willing to sacrifice. Lessons 1.7 and 5.9. 5 hours, read everything first.
## Build it first
- [ ] Threat-model your MQTT node on one page: assets, attackers, entry points, and what each mitigation costs
- [ ] Dump your own firmware over USB with the flashing tool and search it for strings. What did you find?
- [ ] On the sacrificial board only: enable flash encryption in **development** mode and repeat the dump
- [ ] Encrypt the NVS partition and confirm stored credentials are unreadable in a dump
- [ ] Read, do not yet enable, the secure boot procedure. List every irreversible step
## How it works
**Threat modelling** asks: what is worth protecting, from whom, and by which route? Answers drive everything else.

**Secure boot** makes the chip run only firmware signed with your key: the bootloader verifies the app, and the ROM verifies the bootloader, anchored in a key digest burned into **eFuses**. **Flash encryption** makes the contents of flash unreadable without a key held in eFuses. **NVS encryption** protects stored credentials.

eFuses are one-time programmable. A wrong step in release mode permanently locks or bricks the chip, which is why you practise in development mode on a board set aside for it.

Keys are the real problem: where the signing key lives, who can use it, and what happens if it leaks. Software cannot fix a signing key in a public repository.
## Go deeper
- [ ] ESP-IDF release notes for 2026 disabled one secure-boot scheme on some newer chips after a vulnerability. What does that tell you about planning for security updates?
## When to use it, when not to
| Product | Minimum |
| --- | --- |
| Hobby project | TLS with verification, no secrets in the repository |
| Shipped product | Secure boot, flash encryption, per-device credentials, signed OTA |
## Break it
- [ ] Find a secret in your own Git history.
## Check yourself
1. What does secure boot guarantee?
2. What does flash encryption protect against?
3. Why are eFuse operations dangerous?
## Stretch goals
- Give each device its own certificate instead of a shared password.
## Reading
ESP-IDF guide: “Security Overview”, “Secure Boot v2”, “Flash Encryption”.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **One password for the whole fleet.**
- **Interview angle.** “How would you secure an IoT device?” Start with the threat model.

5.11.body:
## Why this matters
Wi-Fi and BLE are not the only radios. Long range at tiny data rates, and mesh networks for buildings, are whole product categories you should be able to place.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Two LoRa modules if you bought them; otherwise read-only. 3 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] With modules: wire one to each board over SPI, send a counter point to point, and measure range in the open and through walls
- [ ] Vary the spreading factor and record range, time on air and data rate
- [ ] Without modules: compute time on air for a 20-byte packet at the slowest and fastest settings from a LoRa calculator
- [ ] Either way: fill in a table of Wi-Fi, BLE, LoRa, Zigbee, Thread and cellular by range, data rate, power and infrastructure needed
## How it works
**LoRa** is a radio modulation that trades data rate for range: kilometres, at a few hundred bits per second, on milliwatts. **LoRaWAN** is the network on top: gateways, a network server, and strict duty-cycle rules. In India the band is 865 to 867 MHz.

**Zigbee** and **Thread** are low-power mesh networks on a different radio (802.15.4): devices relay for each other. **Matter** is an application standard for smart-home devices that runs over Thread and Wi-Fi.

**Ethernet** gives a wired, deterministic link; the classic ESP32 has the controller built in and needs only a transceiver. **Modbus TCP** is lesson 3.7’s protocol over that or Wi-Fi.

**Cellular** variants for devices, LTE-M and NB-IoT, give coverage anywhere at the cost of a modem, a SIM and a subscription.
## Go deeper
- [ ] A soil sensor reports 12 bytes every hour from a field 3 km from the house. Choose the radio and justify it against two alternatives.
## When to use it, when not to
See your table: this lesson is the “when” for wireless.
## Break it
- [ ] Transmit continuously on LoRa and work out by how much you exceeded the legal duty cycle.
## Check yourself
1. What does LoRa trade for range?
2. What is the difference between Thread and Matter?
3. When is cellular the right answer?
## Stretch goals
- Join a public LoRaWAN network if one covers you.
## Reading
Semtech’s “LoRa and LoRaWAN” introduction. The Thread Group’s overview.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Choosing a radio before knowing the payload, range and power budget.**
- **Interview angle.** “Which wireless technology for this product, and why?”

6.1.body:
## Why this matters
Settings, calibration and counters must survive power loss. NVS is the small, safe key-value store every ESP-IDF product uses for that.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lesson 1.7. 2 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Store a boot counter and increment it each start
- [ ] Store a settings struct as a blob with a version number in it
- [ ] Pull the power during a write, many times. Is the data ever corrupt?
- [ ] Fill the partition and handle the error
- [ ] Erase NVS from the command line and confirm the defaults return
## How it works
NVS stores named values in a flash partition. Flash can only be erased a block at a time and wears out, so NVS appends new entries and reclaims old pages later: a small log-structured store with **wear levelling** built in. Writes become durable when you commit.

Version your stored data. A firmware update that reads last year’s struct layout is a common field failure, and rollback makes it two-directional.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Your settings struct gains a field. Write the migration, and say what an older firmware does when it meets the new format.
## When to use it, when not to
| Data | Store in |
| --- | --- |
| Small settings, keys, counters | NVS |
| Files, logs, assets | A file system |
| Values that change every second | RAM, saved occasionally |
## Break it
- [ ] Write a value a thousand times a second and compute how long the flash would last.
## Check yourself
1. Why can flash not be overwritten in place?
2. What is wear levelling?
3. Why version stored data?
## Stretch goals
- Keep factory calibration in a separate, read-only NVS partition.
## Reading
ESP-IDF guide: “Non-Volatile Storage Library”.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Saving on every change.**
- **Interview angle.** “How do you store configuration reliably on flash?”

6.2.body:
## Why this matters
Logs, web pages, audio and models are files. Three file systems are on offer and they fail differently when the power goes.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lessons 3.3 and 6.1; an SD card. 4 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Mount LittleFS on a flash partition; write, read and list files with the standard C functions
- [ ] Mount FAT on the SD card and do the same
- [ ] Time writing 1 MB in 64-byte chunks and in 4 KB chunks on each
- [ ] Cut power during writes fifty times. Which file system needs repair?
- [ ] Log sensor data with a pattern that survives power loss: append, flush, rotate files
## How it works
A file system maps names to blocks and survives, or does not, an interrupted write.

**FAT** is readable by every computer, which is why SD cards use it. It was not designed for power cuts and can lose files or corrupt its tables. **LittleFS** was designed for microcontrollers: it is power-loss safe and wear-levelled. **SPIFFS** is older and has no real directories.

SD cards connect by SPI or by the faster native SDMMC interface, and contain their own controller that sometimes pauses for tens of milliseconds.

Write in large blocks. Small writes are slow and wear flash faster.
## Go deeper
- [ ] How do you make “replace this file with a new version” safe against power loss at any instant?
## When to use it, when not to
| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Internal flash, robustness | LittleFS |
| Removable card, PC-readable | FAT |
## Break it
- [ ] Pull the SD card out during a write.
## Check yourself
1. Why is FAT risky on a device that loses power?
2. Why write in large blocks?
3. What does the write-then-rename pattern achieve?
## Stretch goals
- Serve the files over the web server from lesson 5.6.
## Reading
ESP-IDF guide: “FAT Filesystem Support”, “SD/SDIO/MMC Driver”. The LittleFS design notes.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Never calling flush.**
- **Interview angle.** “How do you log data so a power cut loses at most one record?”

6.3.body:
## Why this matters
Flash is a fixed budget you divide once. A layout that leaves no room for the next feature, or for the app to grow, cannot be changed on deployed devices.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lessons 1.7 and 5.9. 90 minutes.
## Build it first
::widget memory

- [ ] Design a 16 MB layout for the capstone: two app slots, NVS, factory NVS, a file system, a core-dump partition
- [ ] Leave each app slot at least half as large again as today’s binary
- [ ] Build with it and print the table at boot
- [ ] Write down what you would do if the app outgrew its slot after shipping
## How it works
List what must be stored, estimate each with growth, then place them: small fixed things first, apps aligned to 64 KB, the file system last so it can take the remainder.

The partition table is effectively permanent: an OTA update replaces an app slot, not the table. Changing it in the field means a risky multi-step migration.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Which partitions must never be erased by a factory reset?
## When to use it, when not to
| Partition | Size by |
| --- | --- |
| App slots | Current binary plus generous growth |
| NVS | Number of keys and write frequency |
| File system | Data kept, plus free space for wear levelling |
## Break it
- [ ] Shrink the app slot to exactly today’s size and add one feature.
## Check yourself
1. Why is the layout hard to change later?
2. How much headroom should an app slot have?
3. What goes in a factory-data partition?
## Stretch goals
- Add a script to CI that fails when the binary exceeds 80% of its slot.
## Reading
ESP-IDF guide: “Partition Tables”.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Slots sized to fit today’s build.**
- **Interview angle.** “How would you lay out flash for an OTA-capable product?”

6.4.body:
## Why this matters
The crash that matters happens in a customer’s house with no cable attached. Logs and core dumps are how the device tells you what went wrong afterwards.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lessons 1.15 and 6.3. 3 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Give each module its own log tag; set levels per tag at run time
- [ ] Enable core dumps to flash. Cause a crash, reboot, and extract the dump
- [ ] Open it with the analysis tool: see every task’s backtrace and the faulting line
- [ ] Record the reset reason and a boot counter; report both over MQTT after reconnecting
- [ ] Measure how long a log line takes, and what verbose logging does to a timing-critical task
## How it works
**Logging** has levels (error, warning, info, debug, verbose) and tags. Levels compiled out cost nothing; levels filtered at run time still cost a check. A log line is a slow, blocking write to a UART.

A **core dump** is a snapshot of every task’s stack and registers at the moment of a crash, saved to a flash partition. With the matching build files, the tools reconstruct backtraces as if you had been debugging live. Keep the build outputs of every released version.

Field diagnostics are a pipeline: detect, capture, survive the reboot, upload, and match to a firmware version.
## Go deeper
- [ ] What must you archive at release time to be able to read a dump a year later?
## When to use it, when not to
| Tool | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Logs | Normal operation, expected errors |
| Core dump | Crashes |
| Counters and reset reasons | Fleet-wide health |
## Break it
- [ ] Try to analyse a dump with the build files from a different version.
## Check yourself
1. What does a core dump contain?
2. Why keep build outputs for every release?
3. What does logging cost at run time?
## Stretch goals
- Upload dumps automatically after the next successful connection.
## Reading
ESP-IDF guide: “Core Dump” and “Logging library”.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Logging secrets.**
- **Interview angle.** “How do you debug a crash you cannot reproduce?”

6.5.body:
## Why this matters
“How long will the battery last?” has an answer you can compute before building and measure afterwards. Being within 15% is the mark of someone who understands the whole system.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
A battery, a protected charger board, a power meter or INA219. Lesson 2.12. 5 hours.
## Build it first
::widget power

- [ ] List every state of your node (sleep, wake, sense, connect, transmit) with its current and duration, measured, not assumed
- [ ] Enter them in the lab and predict battery life
- [ ] Run the node for a day and compare consumed charge with the prediction
- [ ] Find the largest contributor and halve it
- [ ] Trigger a brown-out by supplying the board through a long thin wire and transmitting; read the reset reason
## How it works
Average current is the sum of each state’s current times its share of time. The battery’s capacity divided by that is the life, reduced by self-discharge, temperature and the regulator’s efficiency.

**Peak current** matters separately: a radio burst of hundreds of milliamps makes the battery voltage dip. If it falls below the chip’s limit, the **brown-out detector** resets the system. Capacitors near the chip supply the peak.

Lithium cells are dangerous when over-charged, over-discharged or shorted. Use cells with a **protection circuit**, a proper charger chip, and never charge unattended.
## Go deeper
- [ ] The regulator on your dev board wastes more than the chip uses in sleep. What would you change on a custom board?
## When to use it, when not to
| Lever | Typical gain |
| --- | --- |
| Shorter awake time | Large |
| Longer sleep interval | Large |
| Lower sleep current | Matters only once the above are done |
## Break it
- [ ] Leave Wi-Fi modem sleep off and remeasure.
## Check yourself
1. How is average current computed?
2. What causes a brown-out reset?
3. Why does peak current matter as well as average?
## Stretch goals
- Report battery voltage with each message and plot the discharge curve.
## Reading
The power-consumption section of the ESP32-S3 datasheet. *Making Embedded Systems*, “Reducing Power Consumption”.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Trusting datasheet currents for a dev board.**
- **Interview angle.** “Estimate the battery life of this design.”

6.6.body:
## Why this matters
Firmware that works on the desk and resets next to a motor is failing an electrical test. You do not need to be an EMC engineer; you need to recognise the symptoms.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
A motor or relay, a scope if you have one. 2 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Switch a small motor or relay near your I2C wires and count bus errors
- [ ] Wind three turns of wire onto a scope probe as a pickup loop and move it over the board while transmitting
- [ ] Add a diode across the relay coil and a capacitor across the motor; repeat the test
- [ ] Shorten and twist the sensor wires; repeat
## How it works
Fast-changing currents radiate and couple into nearby wires. Long wires are antennas, both ways. The usual fixes are physical: short return paths, a solid ground, decoupling capacitors, twisted pairs, a diode across every coil.

**ESD** is the spark from your finger: thousands of volts for nanoseconds. It can reset a device or damage a pin permanently. Connectors exposed to users need protection parts.

Firmware’s share: filter inputs, check CRCs, retry, and recover with a watchdog. And do not make noise: slower edges where speed is not needed.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Why does a diode across a coil stop the spike?
## When to use it, when not to
Suspect EMC when a fault correlates with something else switching, with cable length, or with touching the device.
## Break it
- [ ] Remove the decoupling capacitor nearest a sensor.
## Check yourself
1. What makes a wire an antenna?
2. What is ESD?
3. Name two firmware defences against electrical noise.
## Stretch goals
- Read the layout guidelines in Espressif’s hardware design guide.
## Reading
Espressif’s “Hardware Design Guidelines” for the ESP32-S3.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Fixing a hardware problem with a software retry and calling it done.**
- **Interview angle.** “The device resets when the motor starts. Where do you look?”

6.7.body:
## Why this matters
You will work with hardware engineers and review their schematics. Designing one small board teaches you what to ask for and what your firmware depends on.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
KiCad on your computer. Lessons 0.6 and 6.6. 8 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Draw the schematic of a carrier for an S3 module: USB connector, regulator, reset and boot buttons, one I2C sensor, an LED
- [ ] Copy the module’s reference circuit from Espressif’s guide; note every part you do not understand and look it up
- [ ] Add decoupling capacitors at every supply pin and pull-ups where the datasheet requires
- [ ] Lay out the board on two layers: ground plane, short decoupling paths, nothing under the antenna
- [ ] Run the design-rule check to zero errors
- [ ] Write the pin table your firmware will need
## How it works
A **schematic** says what connects to what. A **layout** decides where the copper goes, which determines whether it works at speed and near a radio.

The essentials for a module-based design: follow the reference circuit; decouple every supply pin close to it; keep the **antenna keep-out** clear of copper and parts; give USB’s two data lines a matched, short route; choose strapping-pin connections so the board boots.

Bring out test points for power, reset, the boot pin and the serial lines. Firmware bring-up starts there.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Which firmware features would be impossible if a strapping pin were tied the wrong way?
## When to use it, when not to
| Stage | Hardware |
| --- | --- |
| Learning, prototyping | Dev boards and breadboards |
| Field trials, small production | A custom board around a certified module |
## Break it
- [ ] Put a ground pour under the antenna in the layout and read what the guide says it does.
## Check yourself
1. What is an antenna keep-out?
2. Why place decoupling capacitors close to pins?
3. What should a firmware engineer ask to be added to a board?
## Stretch goals
- Order five boards and bring one up.
## Reading
Espressif’s hardware design guidelines. Phil’s Lab’s KiCad series.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **No test points.**
- **Interview angle.** “How do you work with the hardware team during bring-up?”

## Why this matters
Unit tests cover logic. Products fail at the seams: the driver against the real chip, the firmware against the real server. A test strategy says what is tested where.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lessons 1.14 and 1.16. 4 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Sort every check you can think of for the capstone into: host unit test, on-target test, hardware-in-the-loop, manual
- [ ] Write an on-target test with the Unity component for the I2C driver against the real sensor
- [ ] Write a Python test that flashes the board, sends shell commands and asserts on the replies
- [ ] Add one hardware-in-the-loop check: the script toggles a pin through a second board and expects a reaction
- [ ] Run the lot with one command
## How it works
The **test pyramid**: many fast unit tests on the host; fewer integration tests on the chip; a few end-to-end tests of the whole device.

**Hardware-in-the-loop** drives the real device’s inputs and checks its outputs automatically. **Software-in-the-loop** runs the real code against a simulated world, as with QEMU or a fake HAL.

Each level catches what the one below cannot: a unit test cannot find a wrong pull-up, and an end-to-end test cannot tell you which line is wrong.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Which bug from earlier phases would each level have caught first?
## When to use it, when not to
| Risk | Test at |
| --- | --- |
| Logic, parsing, maths | Host |
| Register sequences, timing | Target |
| Behaviour as a product | Hardware-in-the-loop |
## Break it
- [ ] Make the HIL test flaky on purpose with a race, then make it deterministic.
## Check yourself
1. What does each layer of the pyramid catch?
2. What is hardware-in-the-loop testing?
3. Why not test everything end to end?
## Stretch goals
- Try Espressif’s pytest plug-in for embedded targets.
## Reading
*Test-Driven Development for Embedded C*, the later chapters. ESP-IDF guide: “Unit Testing”.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Only manual testing.**
- **Interview angle.** “What is your testing strategy for firmware?”

## Why this matters
A build that works only on your laptop is a liability. Continuous integration builds and tests every change the same way, every time.

## Why this matters
Firmware lives for years and passes between people. History, versions and reviews are how a team knows what is running on a device and why.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Your repository. 2 hours.

- [ ] Write a changelog entry and a README section a stranger could follow
## How it works
Small commits that each do one thing make history searchable and `git bisect` possible. A commit message explains *why*; the diff already shows what.

A **version** printed at boot, tied to a tag and a hash, is how a log from the field is matched to source.

**Code review** catches design problems and spreads knowledge. Review for correctness, error handling, concurrency and clarity, in that order.
## Go deeper

## Why this matters
Regulated industries, automotive above all, wrap engineering in processes and standards. You will not master them here; you will know what the acronyms mean when a posting lists them.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
None. 2 hours of reading.
## Build it first
- [ ] Map your capstone onto a V-model: requirements, design, implementation on the way down; unit, integration and system tests on the way up, each paired with its level
- [ ] Write three requirements for the capstone that are testable, with the test for each
- [ ] Pick five MISRA C rules and find a violation of each in your own code
- [ ] Write two sentences each on ISO 26262, IEC 61508 and AUTOSAR
## How it works
**Agile and Scrum** organise work into short iterations with a prioritised backlog. The **V-model** pairs every design stage with a verification stage, and is the shape regulated projects must demonstrate.

**IEC 61508** is the general standard for functional safety of electronic systems. **ISO 26262** adapts it to road vehicles and defines integrity levels, ASIL A to D, that dictate how rigorous development must be. **MISRA C** is a coding standard that restricts C to a safer subset.

**AUTOSAR** is a standardised software architecture for vehicle control units: applications sit above a run-time layer and standardised basic software, so components move between suppliers.

The common thread is **traceability**: every requirement linked to its design, code and test.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Which practices from this course would a safety auditor ask to see evidence of?
## When to use it, when not to
| Domain | Expect |
| --- | --- |
| Consumer IoT | Agile, light process |
| Automotive, medical, industrial safety | V-model, standards, audits |
## Break it
- [ ] Find a requirement in your capstone that cannot be tested as written, and rewrite it.
## Check yourself
1. What does the V-model pair?
2. What is an ASIL?
3. What is traceability?
## Stretch goals
- Read one public MISRA-compliance statement from an open-source project.
## Reading
Introductory material on ISO 26262 and AUTOSAR from their publishers. *Making Embedded Systems* on process.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Treating process as paperwork.** It exists because of specific accidents.
- **Interview angle.** “Are you familiar with functional safety?” Be honest about depth; show you know the vocabulary.

## Why this matters
Logging is the first debugging tool and the easiest to misuse: too little and you are blind, too much and you change the timing you are trying to observe.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lesson 6.4. 2 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Time one log line at 115200 baud with a pin toggle. Then at ten times the baud rate
- [ ] Log inside a 1 kHz task and measure its jitter with and without
- [ ] Buffer events in RAM during the critical section and print them afterwards
- [ ] Set the default level to warning and one tag to debug at run time
## How it works
A log line is formatted, then pushed out of a UART at a fixed rate: a hundred characters at 115200 baud is nearly nine milliseconds, during which the calling task waits.

So: log state changes, not steady state. Use levels and tags. Never log from an interrupt. For timing-sensitive paths, record compact events to a ring buffer and print later, or toggle a pin.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Design a binary log format that takes eight bytes per event and is decoded on the computer.
## When to use it, when not to
| Path | Observe with |
| --- | --- |
| Slow, rare | Logs |
| Fast, periodic | Pin and analyzer, or buffered events |
## Break it
- [ ] Add a verbose log to the I2S reader from lesson 3.4 and listen.
## Check yourself
1. Why is logging slow?
2. What should never log?
3. How do you observe a fast path?
## Stretch goals
- Send logs over UDP instead of the UART.
## Reading
ESP-IDF guide: “Logging library”.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **“It works when I add a print.”** You changed the timing.
- **Interview angle.** “How do you debug a timing-sensitive bug?”

## Why this matters
A panic message is a complete crime-scene report if you can read it. Most engineers scroll past it.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lessons 1.11 and 6.4. 3 hours.
## Build it first
Cause each, save the full output, and name the line of code from the output alone:
- [ ] A NULL pointer write
- [ ] A stack overflow
- [ ] A divide by zero
- [ ] A watchdog timeout
- [ ] A heap corruption: write one byte past an allocation, then free it
- [ ] An `abort()` from a failed error check
## How it works
A panic prints: the **exception cause**; the **registers**, including the program counter and the faulting address; and a **backtrace** of return addresses. The monitor turns addresses into file and line using the build’s symbol file.

Reading order: cause first, then the faulting address (near zero means a NULL dereference; a strange value means a wild pointer), then the top few backtrace frames in *your* code.

Heap corruption is the hard one: the crash happens later, in innocent code. Heap integrity checking and poisoning find the culprit earlier.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Why does a stack overflow sometimes show up as a crash in a completely different task?
## When to use it, when not to
Decode every panic before changing any code. Guessing costs more than reading.
## Break it
- [ ] Decode a backtrace against the wrong build and see the nonsense it produces.
## Check yourself
1. What three things does a panic report?
2. What does a faulting address near zero suggest?
3. Why is heap corruption hard to trace?
## Stretch goals
- Enable comprehensive heap poisoning and repeat the corruption test.
## Reading
ESP-IDF guide: “Fatal Errors” and “Heap Memory Debugging”.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Fixing the line that crashed when the line that corrupted is elsewhere.**
- **Interview angle.** “Walk me through how you would diagnose this crash dump.”

## Why this matters
Lesson 1.15 was the first session. This one covers what you reach for on a hard bug: conditions, watchpoints, threads and scripts.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lesson 1.15; an ESP-PROG if you want to debug the classic chip. 3 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Stop only when a queue is full: a conditional breakpoint
- [ ] Find what writes a corrupted global: a watchpoint
- [ ] List all tasks, switch to one, and print its backtrace
- [ ] Attach to a running, hung device without resetting it and find where each task is stuck
- [ ] Write a three-line GDB script that prints a struct every time a function is entered and continues
## How it works
A **conditional breakpoint** evaluates an expression at each hit: precise, but slow in a hot loop. A **watchpoint** uses a hardware comparator and costs nothing until it fires.

OpenOCD understands FreeRTOS, so each task appears as a thread with its own stack. **Attaching** to a hung device, instead of restarting it, preserves the evidence.

GDB can run commands at a breakpoint and continue, turning it into a tracer that needs no rebuild.
## Go deeper
- [ ] A bug appears once an hour. Which of these tools would you leave armed overnight?
## When to use it, when not to
| Symptom | Tool |
| --- | --- |
| Variable has a wrong value | Watchpoint |
| Device hung | Attach and inspect every task |
| Rare path | Conditional breakpoint or scripted trace |
## Break it
- [ ] Set more hardware breakpoints than the chip has and read the error.
## Check yourself
1. Why is a watchpoint cheap?
2. Why attach instead of reset?
3. How do you inspect another task’s stack?
## Stretch goals
- Debug the ESP32-CAM through an ESP-PROG and note the pin conflicts.
## Reading
ESP-IDF guide: “JTAG Debugging”, tips and quirks. The GDB manual on breakpoints.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Resetting a hung device before looking at it.**
- **Interview angle.** “Tell me about the hardest bug you debugged.”

## Why this matters
A leak of sixteen bytes an hour kills a device in a month. You cannot find it by reading code; you find it by measuring.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lesson 1.10. 3 hours.
## Build it first
::widget heap

- [ ] Plant a leak in your MQTT node: one allocation per message that is freed on only one of two paths
- [ ] Log free heap and minimum free heap every minute for an hour and plot them
- [ ] Use heap tracing around the suspect code to list allocations that were never freed, with the call stack of each
- [ ] Fix it and show a flat line
- [ ] Distinguish a leak from fragmentation using the largest-free-block figure
## How it works
A **leak** makes free memory fall steadily. **Fragmentation** leaves free memory steady while the largest block shrinks. They need different fixes.

**Heap tracing** records every allocation and free between two points and reports what is left, with where it was allocated. It is the embedded equivalent of a leak checker.

The usual culprits: an error path that returns early; a buffer handed to a queue that nobody frees; a string built in a loop.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Who owns a buffer passed through a queue? Write the rule down for your project.
## When to use it, when not to
Track free heap and its minimum in every long-running product, and report both as telemetry.
## Break it
- [ ] Free the same pointer twice with heap poisoning enabled.
## Check yourself
1. How do a leak and fragmentation differ in the numbers?
2. What does heap tracing report?
3. Name two common causes of leaks.
## Stretch goals
- Add a heap low-water alarm that logs and restarts cleanly.
## Reading
ESP-IDF guide: “Heap Memory Debugging”.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Testing for ten minutes and declaring no leak.**
- **Interview angle.** “How would you find a memory leak on a device with no OS tools?”

## Why this matters
The glitch that happens once in a thousand transactions will not appear while you watch. Triggers and decoders let the instrument watch for you.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
The logic analyzer; a scope if you have one. Phase 3. 3 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Capture ten seconds of I2C traffic with the protocol decoder on; export the decoded transactions
- [ ] Search the decode for NACKs
- [ ] Inject a fault: a second board briefly pulls SDA low at random. Find the corrupted transaction
- [ ] With a scope: probe the same line and compare a rising edge with what the analyzer showed
- [ ] Measure with a long ground lead and a short one and compare the ringing
## How it works
A **logic analyzer** sees only 0 and 1, on many channels, for a long time: ideal for protocols. A **decoder** turns edges back into bytes and flags framing errors. A **trigger** starts the capture on a condition, so you record the failure and not the hours before it.

An **oscilloscope** sees voltage against time: slow edges, ringing, noise and levels in the undefined band, which a logic analyzer hides by rounding.

Probing changes the circuit. A long ground lead adds inductance and invents ringing that is not there; the probe’s capacitance slows edges.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Your analyzer samples at 24 MHz. What is the fastest SPI clock you can trust it on?
## When to use it, when not to
| Question | Instrument |
| --- | --- |
| What bytes were sent, and when? | Logic analyzer |
| Is the signal electrically healthy? | Oscilloscope |
## Break it
- [ ] Sample a 10 MHz clock at 24 MHz and describe the capture.
## Check yourself
1. What does a logic analyzer hide?
2. What is a trigger for?
3. How can probing mislead you?
## Stretch goals
- Write a script over the exported decode that checks every transaction against expected patterns.
## Reading
The sigrok and PulseView documentation on decoders and triggers.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Trusting a capture taken at too low a sample rate.**
- **Interview angle.** “Which instruments have you used, and for what?”

## Why this matters
When the code is right and the chip misbehaves, the answer is in a document: the reference manual, or the list of the chip’s own bugs.

A reference-manual chapter has a fixed shape: overview, functional description with block diagrams, programming procedures, then the register list. Read the functional description for understanding and the register list for facts.

## Why this matters
Every repetitive check you do by hand is a script waiting to be written. Automation is what lets one engineer look after a product.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lessons 1.16 and 6.8. 3 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Turn your serial test script into `pytest` cases with fixtures that open the port and reset the board

`pytest` discovers test functions, sets up shared resources through **fixtures**, and reports failures precisely. A serial port, a power switch and a second board as stimulus are all just fixtures.

Shell scripts glue tools together and must fail loudly: stop on the first error and return a status the caller can check.

A **regression suite** is the set of tests that must pass before any release. Every field bug should add one.

## Why this matters
The roles at NVIDIA and Qualcomm in your sample are Linux work. The concepts under Linux are the ones you met in FreeRTOS, with one addition that changes everything: memory protection.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
A Linux machine or virtual machine. Phase 4. 4 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Write a C program that forks; print the process IDs; change a variable in the child and show the parent’s is unchanged
- [ ] Do the same with two threads and show that the variable *is* shared
- [ ] Pass data between two processes three ways: a pipe, shared memory, a socket
- [ ] Protect the shared memory with a semaphore
- [ ] Watch a process’s memory map and its threads with the standard tools
## How it works
A **process** has its own virtual address space: it cannot see or corrupt another’s memory, and a crash kills only itself. A **thread** is a flow of execution inside a process, sharing its memory, which is what a FreeRTOS task is.

**Virtual memory** maps each process’s addresses to physical pages through the MMU. It gives isolation, lets programs be larger than RAM, and is why a wild pointer in Linux userspace raises a fault instead of corrupting the system.

Because processes are isolated they need **IPC** to cooperate: pipes, message queues, shared memory, sockets.

The kernel schedules threads much as FreeRTOS does, with more policies and, by default, fairness over strict priority.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Map each FreeRTOS primitive you know to its Linux counterpart.
## When to use it, when not to
| System | OS |
| --- | --- |
| Kilobytes of RAM, microsecond deadlines, milliwatts | RTOS |
| Rich software, many programs, networking stacks, GPUs | Linux |
## Break it
- [ ] Dereference NULL in one process and observe the other carrying on.
## Check yourself
1. What does a process have that a thread does not?
2. What does the MMU provide?
3. Why do processes need IPC?
## Stretch goals
- Give a thread real-time priority and measure its wake-up latency.
## Reading
*Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces*, free online: the chapters on processes and virtual memory.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Assuming Linux is real-time by default.**
- **Interview angle.** “Process versus thread?” and “what is virtual memory?”

## Why this matters
An embedded Linux board boots through a chain much like the ESP32’s, with more stages and a file that describes the hardware.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
QEMU on your Linux machine. Lesson 1.7. 4 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Boot a prebuilt kernel and root file system in QEMU for an ARM board
- [ ] Add U-Boot in front: stop at its prompt, print its environment, and boot the kernel by hand
- [ ] Find the kernel command line and change the console
- [ ] Decompile the device tree and locate the UART and memory nodes
- [ ] Read the kernel’s boot messages and match them to the stages
## How it works
| Stage | ESP32 | Embedded Linux |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fixed in the chip | ROM bootloader | Boot ROM |
| Loader | Second-stage bootloader | U-Boot (often in two parts) |
| Hardware description | Compiled into the firmware | Device tree, a separate file |
| Main software | Your app with FreeRTOS | Kernel, then `init`, then programs |
| Storage layout | Partition table | Partitions and a root file system |

**U-Boot** initialises memory and storage, loads the kernel and the device tree, and passes control. The **device tree** tells one kernel binary which hardware it is on. The kernel then mounts the **root file system** and starts the first process.
## Go deeper
- [ ] What would have to change to boot the same kernel on a different board?
## When to use it, when not to
You meet this chain on every Linux-capable board: Raspberry Pi, Jetson, i.MX.
## Break it
- [ ] Give the kernel the wrong device tree and read where it stops.
## Check yourself
1. What does U-Boot do?
2. What is the device tree for?
3. What does the kernel start first?
## Stretch goals
- Boot over the network with TFTP.
## Reading
Bootlin’s embedded Linux training slides: boot sequence and bootloaders.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Blaming the kernel for a device-tree mistake.**
- **Interview angle.** “Describe the boot process of an embedded Linux system.”

## Why this matters
Embedded Linux is built, not installed: you choose every package and compile it for another processor.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
A Linux machine with 20 GB free. 5 hours, mostly waiting.
## Build it first
- [ ] Cross-compile “hello” for ARM and run it in QEMU
- [ ] Build a minimal system with Buildroot for the QEMU ARM target; boot it
- [ ] Add your program and one library as packages; rebuild
- [ ] Measure the image size and the boot time
- [ ] Read a Yocto recipe and identify its fetch, configure, compile and install steps
## How it works
A **cross-compiler** runs on your computer and produces code for the target. A **build system** automates the whole stack: toolchain, kernel, libraries, programs, and the final image.

**Buildroot** is simple: one configuration, one image, rebuilt from scratch. **Yocto** is layered and far more flexible, used when several products share a base and packages need updates in the field; its learning curve is steep.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Why can you not simply copy binaries from your desktop distribution?
## When to use it, when not to
| Project | Use |
| --- | --- |
| One device, small team | Buildroot |
| Product family, vendor board-support layers, long maintenance | Yocto |
## Break it
- [ ] Run an x86 binary on the ARM target and read the error.
## Check yourself
1. What is cross-compiling?
2. What does a build system produce?
3. When is Yocto worth its complexity?

- Shrink the image below 10 MB.
## Reading
The Buildroot manual’s first chapters. Bootlin’s Yocto training overview.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Hand-modifying the generated image instead of the build.**
- **Interview angle.** “Buildroot or Yocto?”

## Why this matters
On Linux you can reach GPIO, I2C and SPI from an ordinary program. It is the quickest way to bring up a sensor on a Raspberry Pi or a Jetson.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
A Raspberry Pi or similar with your MPU6050. 3 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Toggle a GPIO from the command line with the gpiod tools, then from C
- [ ] Scan the I2C bus and find the MPU6050
- [ ] Read its identity register from C through the i2c-dev interface
- [ ] Port the register logic of your ESP32 driver; only the bus functions change
- [ ] Measure the jitter of a 1 kHz toggle from userspace and compare with the ESP32
## How it works
The kernel exposes buses as device files. A program opens `/dev/i2c-1`, selects a device address and transfers bytes; the kernel’s bus driver does the signalling.

This is convenient and safe, and not real-time: your process can be descheduled at any moment, so microsecond timing is out of reach. That boundary is exactly why systems pair a Linux computer with a microcontroller.

If you kept your driver behind a HAL in lesson 1.12, the port is one file.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Which of your Phase 3 drivers could not work from userspace, and why?
## When to use it, when not to
| Access | From |
| --- | --- |
| Prototyping, slow sensors | Userspace |
| Shared by several programs, interrupts, timing | A kernel driver |
| Hard real-time | A microcontroller |
## Break it
- [ ] Run two programs that talk to the same sensor at once.
## Check yourself
1. How does a program reach an I2C device on Linux?
2. Why is userspace timing poor?
3. What made your driver portable?
## Stretch goals
- Read the sensor from Python and plot it.
## Reading
The Linux kernel documentation for i2c-dev and the GPIO character device.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Bit-banging a timing-critical protocol from userspace.**
- **Interview angle.** “How would you interface a sensor to a Linux board?”

## Why this matters
A device driver is code that runs inside the kernel. Writing the smallest one removes the mystery.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
QEMU or a Raspberry Pi with kernel headers. 4 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Build and load a module that logs on load and unload; read the kernel log
- [ ] Add a character device: a file in `/dev` that returns a message when read
- [ ] Accept writes and store the last message
- [ ] Protect the buffer against two processes at once
- [ ] Crash the kernel deliberately in QEMU and read the report
## How it works
A **module** is code linked into the running kernel. It has an init and an exit function and no `main`.

A **character device** connects file operations (open, read, write, release) to your functions. A program calls `read`; the kernel calls yours.

Kernel code has no memory protection from itself: a wild pointer takes down the whole system. Data must be copied explicitly between user and kernel space, and anything shared needs locking, because several processes and interrupts can enter your driver at once.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Compare this with an ESP-IDF driver: what does the kernel add, and what does it demand?
## When to use it, when not to
Write a kernel driver when hardware must be shared safely between programs, needs interrupts, or fits an existing kernel subsystem.
## Break it
- [ ] Copy to a user pointer without the proper function and observe.
## Check yourself
1. What is a kernel module?
2. What does a character device map?
3. Why is a bug in a driver worse than a bug in a program?
## Stretch goals
- Add an ioctl.
## Reading
*Linux Device Driver Development*, the character-device chapters.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Sleeping while holding a spinlock.**
- **Interview angle.** “What is a character device driver?”

## Why this matters
This is what Linux driver work mostly is: a client driver for a chip on a bus, bound to the hardware by a device-tree node.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
A Raspberry Pi with the MPU6050. Lessons 3.2 and 8.5. 5 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Write a device-tree overlay declaring your sensor on the I2C bus with a compatible string
- [ ] Write an I2C client driver whose probe function runs when the overlay is loaded; read the identity register there
- [ ] Expose acceleration through a file in sysfs
- [ ] Read it from a shell
- [ ] Find the kernel’s existing driver for the same chip and compare its structure with yours
## How it works
The kernel separates **bus drivers**, which know how to signal, from **client drivers**, which know a chip. The device tree says “a chip matching this name is at this address on this bus”; the kernel finds the driver claiming that name and calls its **probe** function.

Your driver then uses the kernel’s I2C functions, and offers its data through a standard interface. Real sensor drivers use the industrial I/O subsystem, so that every accelerometer looks the same to applications.

The register knowledge is the same as in lesson 3.2. Only the framework around it differs.
## Go deeper
- [ ] What does the kernel’s driver handle that yours does not?
## When to use it, when not to
Use an existing kernel driver when there is one. Write your own for new or custom hardware.
## Break it
- [ ] Mistype the compatible string and observe that probe never runs.
## Check yourself
1. What triggers a driver’s probe function?
2. What is a compatible string?
3. Why use a kernel subsystem instead of your own file?
## Stretch goals
- Add interrupt support for the sensor’s data-ready pin.
## Reading
*Linux Device Driver Development*, the I2C client chapter. The kernel’s device-tree bindings documentation.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Hard-coding the bus and address in the driver.**
- **Interview angle.** “How does Linux match a driver to a device?”

## Why this matters
Machine learning on a device starts as a data problem, not a model problem. A firmware engineer who can frame the task, split the data honestly and read a confusion matrix is already ahead of most.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
The gesture recordings from lesson 4.13; Python with a notebook. 6 hours.
## Build it first
::widget cm

- [ ] In the explorer, set 100 events against 900 background windows. Find the threshold with the best accuracy, and note its recall. Then find the threshold you would ship
- [ ] Load your recordings; cut them into one-second windows with a label each
- [ ] Split by *recording session*, not by window: train, validation, test
- [ ] Train a small dense network in Keras on raw windows; plot training and validation loss
- [ ] Print the confusion matrix on the test set. Which two gestures are confused?
- [ ] Record a new session on another day and test again
## How it works
**Framing.** Decide what goes in (one second of six IMU channels), what comes out (one of four classes), and what a mistake costs in each direction.

**Splits.** The model is fitted on the training set, tuned on the validation set, and judged once on the test set. Windows cut from one recording are near-duplicates, so splitting by window leaks the answer and inflates the score. Split by session or by person.

**Overfitting.** Training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises: the model is memorising. Remedies: more varied data, a smaller model, regularisation, stopping early.

**Metrics.** Accuracy misleads when classes are unbalanced. **Precision** is how often an alarm is right; **recall** is how many real events are caught. A product specification states both, usually as “misses per hundred” and “false alarms per hour”.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Your model scores 98% in the notebook and 70% on the new day’s data. List three causes and how you would test each.
## When to use it, when not to
| Problem | Approach |
| --- | --- |
| A threshold on one signal works | Use the threshold. No model |
| Patterns across time or channels, hard to write as rules | A small model |
## Break it
- [ ] Split by window instead of by session and compare the two test scores.
## Check yourself
1. Why split by session?
2. What does rising validation loss mean?
3. When is accuracy the wrong metric?
## Stretch goals
- Add a “none of the above” class and see what it does to false alarms.
## Reading
*AI at the Edge*, the chapters on datasets and evaluation. *TinyML*, chapters 1 to 3.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Tuning on the test set.** It stops being a test.
- **Interview angle.** “How do you know your model will work in the field?”

## Why this matters
Raw samples are a poor input for a small model. A few lines of signal processing turn them into features that make a tiny network sufficient, and that is where a firmware engineer adds most value.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lessons 0.8 and 3.4. 6 hours.
## Build it first
::widget fft

- [ ] In the viewer, compare rectangular and Hann windows on a tone between two bins
- [ ] In Python, compute a spectrogram of a recorded clap and of speech; look at both
- [ ] On the device, compute a 256-point FFT of accelerometer data with the DSP library and print the three strongest bins
- [ ] Tape the IMU to a fan and find the rotation frequency
- [ ] Time the FFT on the device, and compare float against fixed point if the library offers both
- [ ] Retrain your gesture model on simple features (mean, variance, energy in four bands) and compare size and accuracy with raw input
## How it works
**Windowing** cuts the stream into overlapping frames. **The FFT** turns a frame into energy per frequency. A sequence of FFTs over time is a **spectrogram**: an image a small convolutional network can read.

For speech, energies are grouped into **mel** bands spaced like human hearing and compressed logarithmically; the further-compressed form is **MFCC**. For vibration, band energies and a few statistics are often enough.

**Filtering** removes what you do not want before it reaches the model: gravity from an accelerometer, mains hum from an analog input.

Every feature costs time and RAM on the device, every time. The feature pipeline in the notebook and on the chip must match exactly, or accuracy silently falls.
## Go deeper
- [ ] With 16 kHz audio, 30 ms frames and a 10 ms hop, how many frames per second, and how many bytes for one second of 40 mel bands?
## When to use it, when not to
| Signal | Typical features |
| --- | --- |
| Motion | Statistics and band energies per window |
| Vibration | Spectrum |
| Audio | Log-mel spectrogram or MFCC |
| Images | Usually none: resize and normalise |
## Break it
- [ ] Use a different window length on the device from the one used in training.
## Check yourself
1. What is a spectrogram?
2. Why window before an FFT?
3. Why must the feature code match in both places?
## Stretch goals
- Run the on-device features over a recorded file and compare with Python’s output number for number.
## Reading
*TinyML*, the audio feature chapters. The esp-dsp documentation.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **A feature mismatch between training and device.** The commonest cause of “it worked in the notebook”.
- **Interview angle.** “What preprocessing would you use for keyword spotting, and why?”

## Why this matters
A model is only as good as the data it saw, and collecting data from a device is firmware work: correct rates, no dropped samples, honest labels.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lessons 4.4 and 6.2. 5 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Extend your logger: fixed sample rate from a hardware timer, a sequence number per sample, a count of dropped samples
- [ ] Save to SD with metadata: device, firmware version, sensor range and rate, who, where, when
- [ ] Label at capture time with a button, not afterwards from memory
- [ ] Collect from three people, in three places, on three days
- [ ] Write the dataset’s own datasheet: what is in it, how it was gathered, what it does not cover
- [ ] Keep the raw data immutable and version the processing scripts
## How it works
Good data is **representative** of where the product will be used, **balanced** enough across classes, and correctly labelled. Variety beats volume: ten people for a minute each teach a model more than one person for an hour.

Failures to guard against: samples dropped by a busy logger; sample rates that drift; labels offset in time; all of one class recorded in one session, so the model learns the session.

**Drift.** The world changes after you ship: new users, wear, seasons. Plan to collect samples from the field and re-evaluate.
## Go deeper
- [ ] How would you detect, on the device, that incoming data no longer looks like the training data?
## When to use it, when not to
Collect your own data whenever the sensor, its mounting or its users differ from a public dataset’s, which is nearly always.
## Break it
- [ ] Train on data from one person and test on another.
## Check yourself
1. Why does variety matter more than volume?
2. What metadata must accompany a recording?
3. What is drift?
## Stretch goals
- Add an “upload this window” command for hard cases found in use.
## Reading
*AI at the Edge*, the dataset chapters.
## Common mistakes and interview angles

- **Interview angle.** “How did you build your dataset, and what are its limits?”
