## Why this matters
Quantization is what makes models fit: a quarter of the size, several times the speed on your S3, and the reason the vector instructions matter. It is also plain fixed-point arithmetic from lesson 0.12.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lessons 0.12 and 9.1. 5 hours.
## Build it first
::widget quant

- [ ] In the lab, set the range to −1.5 to 2.5 at 8 bits. Compute the scale and zero-point by hand and check
- [ ] Add an outlier to the range and watch the step size grow
- [ ] Convert your Keras model to a float TFLite file and note its size
- [ ] Convert again with full-integer quantization, giving the converter a representative sample of your data
- [ ] Evaluate both on the test set. How much accuracy did quantization cost?
- [ ] Open the quantized file in a model viewer and read the scale and zero-point of one tensor
## How it works
Each tensor’s real values are mapped to 8-bit integers with two numbers: **real = scale × (q − zero_point)**. The converter chooses them from the range each tensor takes on **representative data**, so that data must look like real use.

Weights get one scale per output channel; activations get one per tensor. Arithmetic then runs in integers, with the scales folded into a multiply and a shift.

**Post-training quantization** needs only the trained model and sample data. If accuracy falls too far, **quantization-aware training** simulates the rounding during training so the model learns to tolerate it.

Sensitive spots: a tensor with rare large values, and layers whose inputs have very different ranges.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Why does one outlier in the calibration data hurt every other value in that tensor?
## When to use it, when not to
| Target | Format |
| --- | --- |
| Microcontroller | int8, fully quantized |
| Accuracy collapses after PTQ | Quantization-aware training |
| Float is fast enough and RAM is plentiful | Rare on this class of chip |
## Break it
- [ ] Calibrate with random noise instead of real data and evaluate.
## Check yourself
1. Write the formula relating real values to quantized ones.
2. What is representative data for?
3. When do you need quantization-aware training?
## Stretch goals
- Quantize to 16-bit activations and compare.
## Reading
The LiteRT (TensorFlow Lite) documentation on post-training quantization. *TinyML* on optimisation.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Forgetting to quantize the input** on the device with the input tensor’s own scale and zero-point.
- **Interview angle.** “Explain int8 quantization and its effect on accuracy.”

## Why this matters
This is the centre of the course: your own trained model running on your own board, measured.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lessons 4.13 and 9.4. 6 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Convert the quantized model to a C array and add it to a project with the TFLite Micro component
- [ ] Register only the operators your model uses
- [ ] Find the smallest tensor arena that works, then add a margin
- [ ] Feed a recorded test window from flash and check the output matches the notebook
- [ ] Then live: IMU task, window buffer, features, inference, result on the display
- [ ] Time `Invoke()` with the optimised kernels on and off; repeat on the ESP32-CAM’s chip
- [ ] Record flash size, arena size, time per inference and stack high-water mark in a table
## How it works
The **model** is a read-only array in flash. The **interpreter** reads it once, plans every tensor’s place in the **arena**, and thereafter allocates nothing. The **op resolver** links in only the kernels you registered, which keeps the binary small.

One inference: write quantized input into the input tensor, invoke, read the output tensor and dequantize.

On the S3, Espressif’s optimised kernels use the chip’s vector instructions; the component’s own figures show person detection falling from seconds to tens of milliseconds. Your measurement on your model is what counts.

Verify in stages: the same input must give the same output in the notebook’s TFLite interpreter and on the device, before you connect a live sensor.
## Go deeper
- [ ] The arena sits in internal RAM. What happens to inference time if you move it to PSRAM, and why?
## When to use it, when not to
| Runtime | Choose when |
| --- | --- |
| TFLite Micro | Portability across chips, large community |
| ESP-DL | Espressif chips only, PyTorch or ONNX workflow (lesson 9.7) |

## Reading

## Why this matters
A model that does not fit is not a model. Budgeting size, RAM and latency, and knowing which lever moves which, is the engineering half of edge AI.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lesson 9.5. 5 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Write your budget: flash, arena, milliseconds per inference, with the reasons for each number
- [ ] Train three sizes of the same network; plot accuracy against arena size and latency
- [ ] Prune one model and fine-tune it; compare size and speed honestly
- [ ] Distil the large model into the small one and compare with training the small one directly
- [ ] If post-training quantization cost you accuracy, apply quantization-aware training
- [ ] Choose one model and justify it against the budget
## How it works
| Lever | Reduces | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Smaller architecture | Flash, RAM, time | Accuracy |
| Quantization | Flash ×4, time | A little accuracy |
| Pruning | Flash, if stored sparsely | Little speed gain without sparse kernels |
| Distillation | Nothing directly; it makes a small model more accurate | Training effort |
| Smaller input | RAM and time, sharply | Detail |

**RAM** is set by the largest pair of consecutive activation tensors, not by the number of weights. **Latency** follows the number of multiply-accumulates. **Flash** follows the parameter count.

Input size is the strongest lever: halving an image’s side quarters the work.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Your model has few parameters and a huge arena. Which layer is responsible?
## When to use it, when not to
Decide the budget before training, from the product: battery, response time, the other things the chip must do.
## Break it
- [ ] Pick the most accurate model regardless of budget and try to run it.
## Check yourself
1. What determines arena size?
2. Which lever cuts latency most?
3. What does distillation do?
## Stretch goals
- Automate the sweep and plot the trade-off curve.
## Reading
*AI at the Edge* on optimisation. *TinyML*, “Optimizing Latency” and “Optimizing Model and Binary Size”.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Optimising parameter count when RAM is the binding limit.**
- **Interview angle.** “The model is too slow on the target. What do you try, in order?”

Espressif’s own inference library is built for its chips and for a PyTorch-centred workflow. Knowing a second runtime lets you choose, and postings ask for more than one.

## Why this matters
Edge Impulse compresses the whole workflow, data to deployable library, into a browser. It is fast for a first result, and understanding what it generates keeps you in control.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
An account; your logger. Lesson 9.5. 4 hours.

An **impulse** is the pipeline: windowing, a signal-processing block, a learning block. The platform trains it, estimates its cost on a named target, and exports portable C++ containing both the features and the model, so training and device match by construction.

Its compiler can turn the model into plain code without an interpreter, saving RAM.

## Why this matters
Vision is where memory runs out. A camera pipeline is a sequence of buffers, and getting their sizes, formats and ownership right is most of the work.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
An ESP32-CAM or an S3 camera board. Lessons 3.10 and 9.5. 8 hours.
## Build it first
- [ ] Capture a greyscale frame at a small size and print where its buffer lives
- [ ] Resize to the model’s input (96×96 for the standard person-detection model) and convert to int8 with the input tensor’s scale
- [ ] Run the person-detection model and print both scores
- [ ] Time each stage: capture, resize, inference
- [ ] Use two frame buffers so capture continues while you process
- [ ] Add a decision rule: several positive frames in a row before reporting
- [ ] Measure frames per second and peak RAM, on the S3 and on the classic chip
## How it works
The stages: sensor to frame buffer by DMA; **preprocess** (crop, resize, convert colour, normalise, quantize); inference; **postprocess** (threshold, smooth over time).

Frame buffers go in **PSRAM**: there is nowhere else for them. The model’s arena should stay in fast internal RAM if it fits.

**Double buffering** lets the camera fill one buffer while you read another. If processing is slower than capture, drop frames deliberately and always take the newest.

Preprocessing is often slower than you expect, and a mismatch with training (channel order, value range) quietly ruins accuracy.

Espressif’s vision framework packages detection and recognition examples built on this same pipeline.
## Go deeper
- [ ] 96×96 greyscale in, two scores out. How many bytes cross each stage boundary?
## When to use it, when not to
| Task | Approach on this class of chip |
| --- | --- |
| Is there a person? | Classification at low resolution |
| Where is the object? | A detector designed for microcontrollers, at low frame rate |
| Reading text, recognising many classes | Send the frame to a larger machine |
## Break it
- [ ] Feed RGB data to a model trained on greyscale.
## Check yourself
1. Where do frame buffers live, and why?
2. What does double buffering solve?
3. Name two preprocessing mistakes that hurt accuracy.
## Stretch goals
- Wake from sleep on motion, classify, and sleep again.
## Reading
The person-detection example in esp-tflite-micro. ESP-WHO’s documentation.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Optimising the model when resizing is the bottleneck.**
- **Interview angle.** “Describe an image pipeline on a memory-constrained device.”

9.10.body:
## Why this matters
A model that drains the battery in a day is not deployable. Energy per inference, and how often you run one, is the last budget.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
Lessons 6.5 and 9.5. 4 hours.
## Build it first
::widget power

- [ ] Measure current during inference and its duration; compute millijoules per inference
- [ ] Compare CPU at full speed against a lower frequency: is slower cheaper per inference?
- [ ] Duty-cycle: sleep, wake, sample one window, infer, sleep. Compute and then measure the average current
- [ ] Add a cheap first stage: a threshold on signal energy that wakes the model only when something is happening
- [ ] Estimate battery life for one inference per second and for one per minute
## How it works
**Energy = power × time.** A faster inference at higher power often costs less energy than a slow one, because the chip can sleep sooner: “race to idle”.

**Cascades** save the most. A trivial detector runs always; the expensive model runs only when it fires. This is how every always-listening device works.

On the S3, quantized models use the vector instructions; float models do not. Arenas in PSRAM are slower, so the chip is awake longer.

The whole system matters: a sensor that draws a milliamp continuously can dominate a model that runs for 20 ms a second.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Your wake-word model runs 20 times a second. Design a two-stage cascade and estimate the saving.
## When to use it, when not to
| Requirement | Design |
| --- | --- |
| Always watching, battery powered | Cascade plus duty cycling |
| Occasional decision | Deep sleep between inferences |
## Break it
- [ ] Leave the sensor powered through sleep and remeasure.
## Check yourself
1. What is “race to idle”?
2. How does a cascade save energy?
3. Why can PSRAM raise energy use?
## Stretch goals
- Report energy per inference in your model card.
## Reading
*AI at the Edge* on power. The S3 datasheet’s current tables.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Measuring the model and forgetting the sensor and radio.**
- **Interview angle.** “How would you run inference continuously on a coin cell?”

9.11.body:
## Why this matters
The ESP32-S3 is one point on a line that runs from tiny Cortex-M chips to Jetson modules with GPUs. Roles ask where you would put a workload, and why.
## Prerequisites, hardware, time
The Nucleo, if you have one. Phase 9 so far. 5 hours, partly reading.
## Build it first
- [ ] Run your gesture model on the Nucleo with the vendor’s model converter or TFLite Micro with CMSIS-NN; compare time and RAM with the S3
- [ ] Fill in a table for a Cortex-M4, the ESP32-S3, a Cortex-M55 with an NPU, a Raspberry Pi 5 and a Jetson Orin Nano: RAM, typical model size, power, price class
- [ ] Place five workloads on that line: wake word, gesture, person presence, object detection at 30 frames per second, a small language model
- [ ] Write one page: where microcontroller-class edge AI ends and Jetson-class begins, with numbers
## How it works
**Cortex-M** chips run TFLite Micro with **CMSIS-NN** kernels. Newer cores add vector extensions, and some pair with a small **NPU** such as Ethos-U that runs supported operators many times faster. Vendors provide converters that turn a model into optimised C for their parts.

**Jetson** is a Linux computer with a GPU. Models are compiled with **TensorRT** into engines for that exact GPU; **CUDA** is the programming layer beneath; **DeepStream** is a pipeline framework for video analytics; **Isaac** is the robotics stack. Memory is measured in gigabytes and power in watts.

The boundary is set by memory and power. Kilobytes of activations and milliwatts: a microcontroller. Megabytes to gigabytes, full-resolution video, large networks: an accelerator or a GPU. Many systems use both, with the small device deciding when to wake the large one.
## Go deeper
- [ ] Design a doorbell: what runs on a microcontroller, what on a Jetson, and what crosses the link?
## When to use it, when not to
| Workload | Platform |
| --- | --- |
| Always-on sensing, small models | Microcontroller |
| Medium vision models at a few frames per second | Microcontroller with NPU, or a small Linux board with an accelerator |
| Multi-camera video, large models | Jetson-class |
## Break it
- [ ] Try to place a model with 50 MB of weights on the S3 and say what stops you first.
## Check yourself
1. What is an NPU?
2. What does TensorRT do?
3. What sets the boundary between MCU-class and GPU-class edge AI?
## Stretch goals
- Build the capstone: a battery-powered, OTA-updatable, MQTT-reporting edge-AI node with a measured power budget, latency benchmarks and a model card.
## Reading
Arm’s CMSIS-NN overview. NVIDIA’s Jetson documentation on TensorRT.
## Common mistakes and interview angles
- **Choosing the platform before sizing the model.**
- **Interview angle.** “Where would you run this model, and why not somewhere else?”

sheets.title: idf.py and PlatformIO, side by side
sheets.body:
Every firmware lab builds two ways from the same files. Use whichever you prefer; lessons say “build and flash” and mean either column. Both use the ESP-IDF framework underneath. Arduino appears only where a lesson compares against it.

| Task | ESP-IDF command line | PlatformIO |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Choose the chip | `idf.py set-target esp32s3` | Pick an environment: `-e esp32s3`, `-e esp32cam` or `-e esp32dev` |
| Build | `idf.py build` | `pio run -e esp32s3` |
| Flash | `idf.py -p PORT flash` | `pio run -e esp32s3 -t upload` |
| Serial monitor | `idf.py -p PORT monitor`, leave with Ctrl+] | `pio device monitor`, leave with Ctrl+C |
| Flash and monitor | `idf.py flash monitor` | `pio run -e esp32s3 -t upload -t monitor` |
| Configuration menu | `idf.py menuconfig` | `pio run -e esp32s3 -t menuconfig` |
| Size report | `idf.py size`, `idf.py size-components` | `pio run -e esp32s3 -t size` |
| Clean everything | `idf.py fullclean` | `pio run -t fullclean` |
| Your saved options | `sdkconfig.defaults`, `sdkconfig.defaults.<target>` | The same files |
| The generated configuration | `sdkconfig` | `sdkconfig.<environment>` |
| Build output | `build/` | `.pio/build/<environment>/` |
| Add a library | `idf.py add-dependency "espressif/mqtt"` | The same `main/idf_component.yml` file, edited by hand |

Three differences worth knowing:

- **Which ESP-IDF you get.** With `idf.py` you install the version you choose. PlatformIO bundles one with its `espressif32` platform. Platform 8.0.0, released on 19 October 2026, ships ESP-IDF 6.1, which is the version this course is written against; the older 6.x platform releases ship ESP-IDF 5.x. Every lab’s `platformio.ini` asks for `espressif32 @ ^8.0.0`, so PlatformIO installs the right one. If a build complains about that line, update PlatformIO itself (`pio upgrade`).
- **Libraries from the component registry.** Labs that need one (USB, camera) declare it in `main/idf_component.yml`. PlatformIO downloads it on the first build, so that build needs an internet connection.
- **Where the source lives.** PlatformIO normally expects `src/`. Each lab’s `platformio.ini` sets `src_dir = main`, so the ESP-IDF layout is kept and nothing is duplicated.
- **The S3 N16R8 board.** The labs use the generic `esp32-s3-devkitc-1` board with the flash size raised to 16 MB. The PSRAM and flash options come from `sdkconfig.defaults.esp32s3`, as they do under `idf.py`.

The `platformio.ini` files have not been run by me: PlatformIO could not be installed where the course was built. If a lab fails, send me the first error it prints.

sheets.title: ESP32-S3 N16R8 pin warnings
sheets.body:
Build your own pin table in lesson 0.6 and trust it over this page: clone boards differ. Rows marked † are from the datasheets as I know them and are re-checked against the Technical Reference Manual when lesson 0.6 is written.

| Pins | Status | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GPIO35, 36, 37 | Do not use | Wired to the octal flash and PSRAM inside the module on R8 variants (Espressif DevKitC-1 user guide) |
| GPIO26 to 32 † | Not available | Flash and PSRAM bus; not broken out |
| GPIO19, GPIO20 | Reserve for USB | USB D− and D+ of the native USB port, which also carries the built-in JTAG |
| GPIO0, 3, 45, 46 † | Avoid | Strapping pins, sampled at reset. GPIO0 low at reset enters download mode |
| GPIO43, GPIO44 † | Avoid if you use the UART console | UART0 TX and RX, connected to the USB-UART bridge |
| GPIO48 or GPIO38 | On-board RGB LED | GPIO48 on DevKitC-1 v1.0, GPIO38 on v1.1; clones vary |
| GPIO39 to 42 † | Usable | Also the external JTAG pins, only relevant if you attach a probe |
| GPIO1, 2, 4 to 18, 21, 47 † | First choice | No boot, USB or memory role on the common variants |

Other rules worth memorising:

- The S3 is a 3.3 V device. A 5 V signal such as the HC-SR04 echo needs a divider or a level shifter.
- ADC2 is shared with Wi-Fi on Espressif chips; use ADC1 pins for analog inputs in any project that uses the radio †.
- The S3 has no DAC. The classic ESP32 has two, on GPIO25 and GPIO26.

sheets.title: Legacy to current ESP-IDF drivers
sheets.body:
ESP-IDF v6.0 removed most of the pre-v5 drivers. Tutorials written before 2026 often use the left-hand column and will not compile on v6. Source: the ESP-IDF v6.0 and v6.1 migration guides.

| Tutorial uses | State in v6 | Use instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `driver/i2c.h` | End of life; removal planned for v7.0 | `driver/i2c_master.h`, `driver/i2c_slave.h` |
| `driver/timer.h` | Removed | `driver/gptimer.h` |
| `driver/rmt.h` | Removed | `driver/rmt_tx.h`, `driver/rmt_rx.h`, `driver/rmt_encoder.h` |
| `driver/adc.h` | Removed | `esp_adc/adc_oneshot.h`, `esp_adc/adc_continuous.h`, `esp_adc/adc_cali.h` |
| `driver/pcnt.h` | Removed | `driver/pulse_cnt.h` |
| `driver/mcpwm.h` | Removed | `driver/mcpwm_prelude.h` |
| `driver/i2s.h` | Removed | `driver/i2s_std.h`, `driver/i2s_pdm.h`, `driver/i2s_tdm.h` |
| Legacy DAC driver | Removed | `driver/dac_oneshot.h`, `driver/dac_continuous.h`, `driver/dac_cosine.h` |
| `esp_dma_capable_malloc()` | Removed | `heap_caps_malloc()` with `MALLOC_CAP_DMA \| MALLOC_CAP_CACHE_ALIGNED` |
| Built-in `mqtt` component | Moved out in v6.1 | Add the managed component `espressif/mqtt` |
| FreeRTOS types appearing after including a driver header | Driver headers no longer include FreeRTOS | Include `freertos/FreeRTOS.h` yourself |

Two behaviour changes that bite silently:

- The new I2C master functions return `ESP_ERR_INVALID_RESPONSE` on a NACK, not `ESP_ERR_INVALID_STATE`.
- The default C library is Picolibc, not Newlib. Code that relied on Newlib-specific behaviour needs checking.

sheets.title: Serial protocols at a glance
sheets.body:
Typical figures for choosing a bus. Each protocol’s Phase 3 module gives the exact limits with their sources.

| Bus | Signal wires | Typical speed | Reach | Devices | Clock | Pick it when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| UART | 2 (TX, RX) | 9600 to a few Mbit/s | Board to board; metres with RS-232 | 2, point to point | None: both ends agree on the baud rate | Debug consoles, GPS, modems, linking two processors |
| RS-485 | 1 differential pair | Up to about 10 Mbit/s over short runs | Hundreds of metres at low speed | Dozens on one pair | None | Industrial sensors, Modbus, noisy environments |
| I2C | 2 (SDA, SCL), open-drain | 100 kbit/s, 400 kbit/s, 1 Mbit/s | One board; limited by bus capacitance | Many, by 7-bit address | Master | Several low-speed sensors on few pins |
| SPI | 3 plus one chip select per device | 1 to tens of Mbit/s | One board | One per chip-select line | Master | Displays, SD cards, fast ADCs, flash memory |
| I2S | 3 (clock, word select, data) | Set by audio rate | One board | Usually one in, one out | Master | Digital audio to and from microphones and amplifiers |
| 1-Wire | 1 plus ground | About 16 kbit/s | Metres | Many, by 64-bit ID | None: timed slots | A few temperature sensors on a long wire |
| CAN | 1 differential pair | Up to 1 Mbit/s (classic) | 40 m at 1 Mbit/s, longer when slower | Many, any can transmit | None: bit-timed with arbitration | Vehicles, robots, anything safety-related |
| USB | 1 differential pair | 12 Mbit/s full speed on the S3 | A few metres | Host plus devices | Embedded in the data | Talking to a computer or phone |

Use the diagram below to see why I2C and SPI differ: change the protocol, scrub through the frame, and read the note under it.

::widget timing

sheets.title: C pitfalls
sheets.body:
The mistakes that survive code review. Each line is one a lesson made you cause on purpose.

| Pitfall | What happens | Instead | Lesson |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `uint8_t a, b; a + b` | Computed as `int`: no wrap until you store it | Cast the result to the type you mean | 1.5 |
| `~mask` on a `uint8_t` | A 32-bit value with the top bits set | `(uint8_t)~mask` | 1.5 |
| Signed compared with unsigned | The signed side is converted; `-1 < 1u` is false | Keep both sides the same signedness | 1.5 |
| `1 << 31` | Signed overflow: undefined | `1u << 31` | 0.11 |
| Shift by the width or more | Undefined | Check the count | 1.5 |
| Signed overflow | Undefined; the compiler may delete your check | Unsigned maths, or check before adding | 1.5 |
| `sizeof` on an array parameter | Size of a pointer | Pass the length | 1.2 |
| Returning the address of a local | Dangling pointer | Caller supplies the buffer | 1.2 |
| Shared flag without `volatile` | Loop never sees the change at `-O2` | `volatile`, or a notification | 1.3 |
| `volatile` treated as atomic | `x++` still loses updates | Critical section or atomic type | 1.3, 4.8 |
| Struct sent over a wire | Padding and byte order differ | Encode and decode byte by byte | 1.4 |
| Bitfields for registers | Layout is compiler-defined | Masks and shifts | 1.4 |
| `REG = REG \| bit` shared with an ISR | Read-modify-write race | Set and clear registers | 0.13 |
| Large local array | Stack overflow, far from the cause | `static`, or allocate once | 1.11 |
| Unchecked `malloc` | Crash on the ten-millionth pass | Check; prefer static pools | 1.10 |
| `printf` in an ISR | Deadlock or watchdog reset | Queue the event to a task | 2.2 |
| Macro arguments used twice | `MAX(i++, j)` increments twice | `static inline` function | 1.6 |
| `=` in a condition | Assigns | Enable warnings as errors | 1.13 |
| `char` assumed signed | Differs by architecture | `int8_t` or `uint8_t` | 1.5 |
| Missing `break` | Falls through | Comment intended fall-through; warnings on | 1.13 |

Compile with `-Wall -Wextra -Werror -Wconversion -Wshadow` on the host and most of this table is caught for you.

sheets.title: FreeRTOS quick reference
sheets.body:
The calls used in Phase 4, as provided by ESP-IDF. Stack sizes are in bytes here; a higher priority number is more urgent.

| Need | Call | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Create a task | `xTaskCreate(fn, "name", stack, arg, prio, &handle)` | `xTaskCreatePinnedToCore` adds a core |
| Steady period | `xTaskDelayUntil(&last, pdMS_TO_TICKS(ms))` | Measured from the last wake-up |
| Simple delay | `vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(ms))` | Measured from now: drifts |
| Stack headroom | `uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark(NULL)` | Smallest free amount ever |
| Queue | `xQueueCreate(len, item_size)`, `xQueueSend`, `xQueueReceive` | Items are copied |
| From an ISR | `xQueueSendFromISR(q, &item, &woken)` then `portYIELD_FROM_ISR()` if woken | Only `FromISR` calls in an ISR |
| Mutex | `xSemaphoreCreateMutex()`, `xSemaphoreTake(m, ticks)`, `xSemaphoreGive(m)` | Has priority inheritance; never in an ISR |
| Binary semaphore | `xSemaphoreCreateBinary()` | A signal, not a lock |
| Notify a task | `xTaskNotifyGive(h)` / `ulTaskNotifyTake(pdTRUE, ticks)` | Fastest; one receiver |
| Notify with a value | `xTaskNotify` / `xTaskNotifyWait` | Bits or a value |
| Event group | `xEventGroupSetBits`, `xEventGroupWaitBits` | Wait for any or all of several bits |
| Software timer | `xTimerCreate`, `xTimerStart` | Callbacks share one task: keep them short |
| Stream buffer | `xStreamBufferSend`, `xStreamBufferReceive` | Bytes, one writer, one reader |
| Critical section | `taskENTER_CRITICAL(&lock)` … `taskEXIT_CRITICAL(&lock)` | `lock` is a `portMUX_TYPE`; a few instructions only |

**Choosing a primitive**

| Situation | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Pass data between tasks | Queue |
| Wake one task, no data | Task notification |
| Protect a shared resource | Mutex |
| Wait on several conditions | Event group |
| Share a few variables with an ISR | Critical section |
| Bytes from an ISR to a task | Stream buffer |

**Timeouts.** `0` returns at once; `portMAX_DELAY` waits for ever; anything between is a deliberate decision about what to do when the wait fails. The tick is 10 ms by default, so `pdMS_TO_TICKS(5)` is zero.

sheets.title: GDB commands
sheets.body:
Start a session with `idf.py openocd` and `idf.py gdb`, or from PlatformIO with `debug_tool = esp-builtin`. Lessons 1.15 and 7.3.

| Do | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Stop at a function | `break app_main` (`b`) |
| Stop at a line | `break main.c:42` |
| Stop only when a condition holds | `break main.c:42 if count == 5` |
| Stop when a variable is written | `watch tick` |
| Run on | `continue` (`c`) |
| Step over a line | `next` (`n`) |
| Step into a call | `step` (`s`) |
| Run until the current function returns | `finish` |
| Print a value | `print tick` (`p`), `p/x value` for hex |
| Print a struct through a pointer | `p *cfg` |
| Change a value | `set var tick = 0` |
| Show the call stack | `backtrace` (`bt`) |
| List tasks | `info threads` |
| Switch to a task | `thread 3` |
| Registers | `info registers` |
| Memory: four words in hex | `x/4xw 0x60004004` |
| Memory: a string | `x/s ptr` |
| List breakpoints; delete one | `info breakpoints`, `delete 2` |
| Run commands at a breakpoint | `commands 1`, then lines, then `end` |
| Reset and halt the chip | `monitor reset halt` |
| Leave | `quit` |

**Notes for the ESP32**

- Code in flash uses hardware breakpoints, and the chip has only a few. Delete those you are not using.
- “optimized out” means the compiler removed or merged the variable. Build with the debug optimisation level for a debugging session.
- Halting the CPU stops the radio and the watchdog feeding. Timing-sensitive bugs need a logic analyzer or logs.
- On the S3, JTAG is on the native USB port, not the UART one.

sheets.title: Under the hood: what each call does
sheets.body:
Every ESP-IDF call you use, traced to the hardware. Each row was read in the ESP-IDF v6.1 source; the lesson that introduces a call adds its row here. A call missing from this page has not been traced yet: trace it yourself with the method below before you rely on what it costs.

## How to trace any call

1. **Header** (`components/<component>/include/...`): the signature and the comment. Note what it promises, not what it does.
2. **Driver** (`components/esp_driver_<x>/src/<x>.c`): argument checks, locks, memory, bookkeeping. Look for `portENTER_CRITICAL`, mutexes, `malloc`, `vTaskDelay`: these decide whether it blocks or may run in an ISR.
3. **HAL** (`components/esp_hal_<x>/include/hal/<x>_hal.h`): usually a macro that forwards to the LL.
4. **LL** (`components/esp_hal_<x>/esp32s3/include/hal/<x>_ll.h`): `static inline` functions that read and write register fields. This is where the work happens.
5. **Registers** (`components/soc/esp32s3/register/soc/<x>_reg.h` and `<x>_struct.h`): names and addresses, which match the Technical Reference Manual.

With PlatformIO the source is in `~/.platformio/packages/framework-espidf/components/`. In VS Code, F12 on a call goes to its definition; repeat until you reach a register.

Questions to answer for every call: which registers does it touch? Does it block, and on what? May an ISR call it? Is it in IRAM? What does it allocate? What happens on bad arguments?

## GPIO

| Call | Underneath | Blocks | ISR | Lesson |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gpio_reset_pin` | Interrupt off, **pull-up on**, pull-down off, input and output off, RTC IO released, GPIO function selected, reservation dropped | No | No | 0.3, 0.14 |
| `gpio_set_direction` | Input: sets `FUN_IE` in the IO MUX register, clears the `GPIO_ENABLE` bit. Output: clears `FUN_IE`, routes signal 256 (plain GPIO) through the matrix, sets the `GPIO_ENABLE` bit. Both select the GPIO function | No | No | 0.3, 0.14 |
| `gpio_set_pull_mode` | Sets or clears `FUN_PU` and `FUN_PD` in the IO MUX register | No | No | 0.5, 0.14 |
| `gpio_config` | The above for every pin in the mask, plus interrupt type and enable. Sets the whole mode, not added to the old one. Warns on a pin already reserved | No | No | 0.5, 2.1 |
| `gpio_set_level` | One store to `GPIO_OUT_W1TS` or `GPIO_OUT_W1TC` (`OUT1` pair for pins 32 and up) | No | Yes; in IRAM only with `CONFIG_GPIO_CTRL_FUNC_IN_IRAM` | 0.3, 0.14 |
| `gpio_get_level` | One load of `GPIO_IN`. Reads 0 when the input path is off | No | Yes; in IRAM only with `CONFIG_GPIO_CTRL_FUNC_IN_IRAM` | 0.5, 0.14 |

## Time

| Call | Underneath | Blocks | ISR | Lesson |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `esp_timer_get_time` | Snapshots the 64-bit SYSTIMER counter, waits for valid, reads low, high, low until consistent, divides by 16 (16 MHz on the S3). Microseconds since boot, monotonic | No | Yes, in IRAM | 0.10, 0.14 |
| `esp_rom_delay_us` | Mask-ROM routine `ets_delay_us`: spins on the CPU cycle count. Interrupts stay enabled, so it can run long | Spins | Yes | 0.9, 0.14 |
| `vTaskDelay(t)` | Task to the delayed list for t ticks, then yield. 0 ticks is only a yield | Yes | No | 0.9, 0.10 |
| `pdMS_TO_TICKS(ms)` | Macro: `ms * configTICK_RATE_HZ / 1000`, integer. 100 Hz default: under 10 ms gives 0 | n/a | n/a | 0.10 |

## LEDC PWM

| Call | Underneath | Blocks | ISR | Lesson |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ledc_timer_config` | Auto clock tries APB, XTAL, RC_FAST; divider = clock ÷ (frequency × 2^resolution) with 8 fractional bits, written to the timer | No | No | 2.4, 0.14 |
| `ledc_channel_config` | Reserves the pin, routes the channel through the GPIO matrix (`output_invert` is the matrix’s invert bit), sets the first duty. `intr_type` is deprecated in v6.1 | No | No | 2.4, 0.14 |
| `ledc_set_duty` | Critical section; writes `duty << 4` to the duty register. Output unchanged until an update | No | No | 2.4, 0.14 |
| `ledc_update_duty` | Sets `duty_start` and the low-speed update bit: new duty from the next PWM period | No | Yes; in IRAM only with `CONFIG_LEDC_CTRL_FUNC_IN_IRAM` | 2.4, 0.14 |
| `ledc_set_duty_and_update` | Both in one critical section, but fails with `ESP_FAIL` unless `ledc_fade_func_install` was called first | No | No | 2.4 |

## Startup and errors

| Call | Underneath | Lesson |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `app_main` | Called by `main_task` (`freertos/app_startup.c`), priority 1, stack `CONFIG_ESP_MAIN_TASK_STACK_SIZE` (3584 by default). Returning deletes the task; the rest of the system keeps running | 0.1, 1.7 |
| `ESP_ERROR_CHECK(x)` | On failure: prints error, file, line and expression, then aborts. With assertions disabled (`NDEBUG`) it evaluates x and checks nothing | 0.1, 1.13 |
| `printf` | C library formats into stdout; at a newline the line goes to the console driver, which may wait for the host | 0.1, 0.14 |
